title: Lovely mom update (after way too long) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jojoco-gw", "author_name": "jojoco", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jojoco-gw", "date": "2023-11-01", "text": "I'm sure many of you have been wondering what has been going on with my mom but were probably scared to ask.  I'm sorry it has taken me so long to give an update, but here it is, finally. Mom is doing just okay. After she left Yale, she went to a rehab center in NYC. We were so excited for the beginning of a great restorative chapter there, but I've learned that rehab centers are not necessarily a great environment for our older loved ones. Rehab is not a medical facility. That needs to be understood. People go there to focus on specific rehabilitation goals and the attention is almost entirely centered on therapy at the expense of physical issues.  Especially if you are older. Doctors visit a few times a week (and that is a high number) so medical issues are sometimes overlooked.  (UTIs, gunky sounding lungs, dehydration, not eating). Mom didn't get better there, partly due to complications like the ones above. She did walk a bit with a tall walker and a lot of support (person on each side and one behind her with a wheelchair) but she absolutely couldn't stand on her own even for a moment.  She also lost a tremendous amout of weight (down to 90 lbs) and battled delirium over and over again. I wish we hadn't sent her. She came home mid October to 24-hr care. Last week she was hospitalized for dehydration and a UTI. What a difference a real hospital can make.  She came home a few days ago and she is on a new medicine that seems to be keeping the delirium at bay (Seroquel, for anyone who might find this info helpful.) One of the side effects of Seroquel is weight gain. Mom now eats like a stoned college kid at 3 am.  Breakfast (today, for example,) was scrambled eggs with cheese, ham and milk thrown in, a large bowl of oatmeal and some yogurt.  Lunch  was a hearty stew-like  soup, chicken salad and yogurt. Dinner was thai chicken curry, yogurt, raspberries and a pb cookie. Plus two boosts a day.  She is making up for lost time. I am vigilant about making sure that she gets protein and healthy fats. Some sweets to be sure, but not many. Our biggest challenge seems to be the brain injury that she suffered. The part of her brain that controls language was damaged. It may get a bit better but it has been three months and her conversational skill are mostly lost. (and this was a woman who wrote poetry and adored language.) Mom has Fluent Aphasia (also called Wernicke's aphasia).  That means she generally sounds like she is taliking fluently with the correct inflections and intonation, but a lot of what she says makes no sense--made up words, etc. She might say \"I think its a good idea to floober rit nottisop swent.\".  I try to pick out the key words, but I am mostly unsuccessful. I will nod and say, \"I'm on it\" and she will smile. Or I'll prod for more info but again, usually unsuccessfully. She can read but we're not sure how much she comprehends. If you ask her a verbal question she generally can't answer. We're using whiteboards to help her narrow down the range of possible topics involved. We also are working with speech therapists but oh, gosh, it is so hard. It is absolutely heartbreaking. Fortunately, Mom is completely non frustrated by all of this. She smiles a lot and is very agreeable. Interestingly, she can sing some old songs (different part of the brain,) so \"When the Saints Go Marching In\" is often heard here. Dad is hanging in there. He is mission driven in his care of Mom but he is also spending more time in his office upstairs working on his own things. That's a good thing. But his memory is not so great so I spend a lot of time explaining things to him. I try not to get impatient but sometimes I have to walk away because I just have to. My siblings and I all pitch in. Dad has only been alone ( Aides still there though) for maybe 4 days total since late July. And none of us even live in NY. We're all very different and I have definitely rubbed some of them the wrong way but we all want what is best for mom. What exactly is bestt remains to be seen. We all have our own agenda for mom but we all agree to follow the path she leads us down. In the meantime, we'll keep on keeping on. It's hard. It sucks and this still feels like a theft. I miss my mom. Sorry so long. I didn't mean to unload like this.", "images": []}

But, there is still sometimes so much oil that the p butter could almost be poured from the jar! After pouring off what oil is on top, what I have found works well to remove more oil from the rest of the jar is to take a paper towel or sturdy paper napkin, wad or fold it up and lay it on top to the p butter iin the jar.   The paper will absorb an awful lot of the oil . You may lose a bit of p butter, but not a very significant amount.   It takes about a day and if there is stil more than I want , I do it a second time. I love p butter and use it quite a bit in cooking also.   I dont remember it being so oily that it is pourable. This will be my first LVP install, and a first over concrete. A contact adhesive is apparently often used for this, but I'm not a fan especially over concrete where the surface can never be absolutely flat. I would like to use a wet set adhesive so as to fill under plank areas that might want to pull back up a 32nd, and polyurethane seems ideal since it'll stick nicely to both cork and concrete, and many will even provide a moisture barrier with a thin continuous layer applied. main_question: {"author_id": "justin-bekker", "author_name": "Justin Bekker", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/justin-bekker", "date": "2023-11-02", "text": "Hello, We recently moved into a 20 year old house in Alberta, Canada. 1200 sq. ft. upstairs and 1400 sq. ft. on the main floor with an unfinished basement. The house is well built with good sealing everywhere and good insulation in the attic. The master bedroom is in the SW corner of the 2nd floor and gets hot in the afternoon. With the blinds closed and the ambient outside temperature around 20\u00b0C, the bedroom gets to 27\u00b0C. The upstairs is very open with vaulted ceilings in two corners of the house and an open catwalk between the other two corners of the house, so the cold air can fall out of the upstairs easily. Fresh air returns in each of the three upstairs bedrooms. The house has two furnaces (one for basement and main floor and one for upstairs). TL:DR - hot upstairs, challenging architecture, good sealing and insulation. We just put in new heat pumps and they are hardly putting a dent in the upstairs temperature (maybe 1 degree). The main floor is a 3.0 ton and the upstairs is a 2.0 ton unit. With the main floor turned off, but the upstairs cooling, the temperature is still getting to 26\u00b0C in the afternoon and the main floor is around 21\u00b0C. The basement is also cold with the furnace room probably around 18\u00b0C. There is some leaking from the ducting in the furnace room, but I taped everything as best I could. The ducting travels about 40 feet in the basement joists, which are all open to the basement, before heading upstairs. It is cold air blowing upstairs, but it can't keep up. TL:DR - 2 ton upstairs heat pump can't cool the upstairs. The basement is cold with about 40 feet of galvanized steel ducting running through the basement joists before turning upstairs. My suspicion is I am losing my cold air to conduction / convection of the ducting in the basement. Is this possible? I have tried closing all the bedroom doors to keep the cold air from falling downstairs, but it doesn't seem to make a difference.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "author_name": "Charles Ross Homes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "date": "2023-11-03", "text": "Hi, Justin, Sizing HVAC equipment using rules of thumb can get you into trouble.  While cooling load calculations would need to be performed to determine the required system cooling capacity, I'm betting your 2nd floor system is undersized.   Here's the logic:  First, let's agree that the basement cooling load is negligible, so the 3-ton system is dealing with 1st floor load only.  Next, consider that the area of the 2nd floor is only 14% less than the 1st floor.  Now consider that the 2nd floor system also has to provide cooling to offset the radiant heat from the attic and the vaulted ceilings areas (the 1st floor system doesn't need to deal with either) plus the windows and walls with SW exposure. Just noticed rust spot on top of my water heater.  The copper pipe near the valve has some rust as well.  The water heater was newly installed about one year ago.  Everything feels dry as of now.  Is this something I need to worry about? Thanks in advance for your help.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/44429cdb05445f1a_9673-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/8272bc8e05445f1d_9673-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jakethewonderdog64", "author_name": "Jake The Wonderdog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jakethewonderdog64", "date": "2023-11-04", "text": "The top of the water heater is not the tank. It is a sheet metal outer skin, under which is insulation and then the tank. Any rust there is cosmetic. The corrosion at the top of the valve may be a combination of sloppy flux and/or a minor leak. That sort of thing does have a habit of getting pinhole leaks in it over time. I'd ask them to come back on that. Yes, get a CO detector. You don't have to obsess over the top of the water heater, just take a gander ever month or so. I think the bulk of that is backdraft. The water vapor from the flue gasses condenses on the cold water, in particular. But you also see the paint blistering around the vent hood from the heat. Backdraft is not a good thing, but I think it's happening because of the damper not opening quickly. If the damper malfunctions completely it's a bigger problem. I'm far more concerned about the venting than I am about a crappy solder job. Help me out with the flue pipe - is it covered with something? Am I just not seeing it correctly? Is this a material that's not used around here? It looks almost like someone used metal tape all over an existing single wall galvanized flue. Also, I call BS on the pressure release valve discharge.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "savanah-fackler", "author_name": "Arlow Ellis", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/savanah-fackler", "date": "2023-11-03", "text": "Hello, I recently moved into my first home so I have no experience at all with landscaping. Does anyone have some ideas of what I could do with my small front yard as far as maybe a flower bed/types of flowers/lighting? I do live in the Midwest, so we have a cold winter approaching. I can handle the porch decor for the most part but I\u2019m struggling with the yard. Thanks!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/73026cf60544e690_4290-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "simplynatural", "author_name": "simplynatural", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/simplynatural", "date": "2023-11-05", "text": "I would add a walkway for people as they step out of the car.  Right now, it looks like they will have to walk on the grass--or step into a snowbank in winter!  The walkway could be centered on the porch so it looks intentional (even though it would not be centered on the door), and the step could be widened to match. I've added a few evergreen plants in a mulched bed left of the door (nothing in bloom because this is a late fall view).  The two mounded shrubs closest to the walk and porch would bloom white in succession in spring, and the earliest to bloom (sweet box) is fragrant.  You could plant bulbs and low perennials or annuals in front of the evergreens for spring and summer flower color. If there is room, a small tree (dogwood? serviceberry? star magnolia?) would add height, additional spring bloom, summer shade, and fall color.  (That's why people are asking for a wider view. Pari r\u00e9ussi pour cette r\u00e9novation compl\u00e8te d'appartement, qui offre aujourd'hui \u00e0 ses occupants un nouveau cocon organis\u00e9 et styl\u00e9 ! L'entr\u00e9e : L'entr\u00e9e a \u00e9t\u00e9 repens\u00e9e dans son organisation afin d'\u00eatre davantage fonctionnelle. Ainsi une penderie avec rangements et banquette a \u00e9t\u00e9 cr\u00e9\u00e9e sur-mesure. La d\u00e9coration a \u00e9t\u00e9 mise en valeur afin de redonner \u00e0 cette pi\u00e8ce toute son importance. La cuisine : L'acc\u00e8s double de la cuisine d'origine a \u00e9t\u00e9 remplac\u00e9 par un acc\u00e8s unique via le s\u00e9jour. La cloison s\u00e9parant la fen\u00eatre de la cuisine et la baie vitr\u00e9e du s\u00e9jour a \u00e9t\u00e9 supprim\u00e9e. Cette restructuration de la cuisine a permis notamment d'optimiser le nombre de placards afin de r\u00e9pondre davantage aux besoins de rangements de la propri\u00e9taire. Le comptoir, ouvert sur le s\u00e9jour est fini par une planche de ch\u00eane clair r\u00e9alis\u00e9e sur-mesure. La chambre parentale : La chambre parentale a \u00e9t\u00e9 enti\u00e8rement r\u00e9am\u00e9nag\u00e9e afin d'optimiser l'espace et d'accueillir un vrai espace de travail. Le bureau et ses rangements ont \u00e9t\u00e9 \u00e9galement repens\u00e9s. Le parquet a \u00e9t\u00e9 r\u00e9nov\u00e9 et le mur principale de la pi\u00e8ce a \u00e9t\u00e9 peint en bleu cobalt afin d'apporter de la couleur et du style \u00e0 l'ensemble. D\u00e9tail t\u00eate de lit - Chambre parentale  La cliente a des insomnies et ne se sent plus \u00e0 l'aise dans l\u2019ambiance de l'\u00e9tage.  Les salles d\u2019eau sont \u00e9galement obsol\u00e8tes avec un \u00e9quipement qui a fait son temps. Nous proposons de concevoir,  dans un esprit contemporain, les espaces tout en gardant l'\u00e2me de l'habitation.     La Chambre Parentale L\u2019esprit de la nature et la gamme des verts sont les fils conducteurs pour la d\u00e9coration. Nous d\u00e9clinons cette teinte pour les soubassements des murs de la chambre dans une tonalit\u00e9 fonc\u00e9e. La modification du placement du lit, des armoires et la disparition de la chemin\u00e9e existante non fonctionnelle optimisent l\u2019espace d\u00e9di\u00e9 au repos. Un panoramique de style exotique de chez Mazureel met en valeur la t\u00eate de lit r\u00e9alis\u00e9e en bois. Elle est habill\u00e9e naturellement d'un rev\u00eatement en palmier tiss\u00e9 de chez CMO. L\u2019\u00e9clairage en Led tant pour les liseuses que pour l\u2019habillage des corniches murales, cr\u00e9e des ambiances diff\u00e9rentes selon l\u2019humeur.     Cr\u00e9ation d\u2019un dressing sur mesure en compl\u00e9ment.   La Chambre de Jeune Fille La fille de la cliente est une jeune \u00e9tudiante. La jeune femme d\u00e9sire garder l\u2019ensemble du lit, des chevets et de l\u2019armoire car elle aime beaucoup ce mobilier de famille de style 1920. Elle souhaite aussi r\u00e9-organiser son coin bureau. Nous proposons pour cette pi\u00e8ce une gamme de pastels doux en associant un ton cr\u00e8me \u00e0 un vert amande pour les soubassements. Ces coloris mettent en valeur le mobilier fonc\u00e9 et apportent plus de lumi\u00e8re dans la chambre. title: Gardening concepts explored and discussed: Overstory Protection | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "upperbaygardener", "author_name": "UpperBayGardener (zone 7)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/upperbaygardener", "date": "2023-11-05", "text": "Part of a very occasional series... As I have explained before, I live just close enough to the Ches. Bay to get a very slight protecting effect from the warmth of the water.  The big freeze that recently swept across much of the lower 48   presented an opportunity to discuss a somewhat related phenomena in more detail.  'Overstory protection' as it's frequently called. In my opinion this term refers to at least a couple related, but different, benefits of having plant material positioned above other plant material.  Of course it is usually a tree's branches, preferably evergreen, but it doesn't have to be.  Even an arbor with a thick growing vine could work as well, as I'm going to demonstrate. As for the freeze, on the first, coldest night of Nov. 2nd, a weather station I randomly selected in a rather built up but not quite fully urban part of Montgomery County, MD, southwest of me, recorded 27.5F/-2.5C.  Mine here in an almost completely rural setting, recorded 30.8F/-0.66C.   Again, the warmth from water roughly a mile away made the difference.  Back to what happened in my garden at those temperatures, though. Here we see that even the overstory protection of a 3.5 ft / 1.1m \"Clerodendrum ugandense\"/Rotheca myricoides protected a tiny sliver of Lantana foliage, preventing it from freezing.  Even the flowers are ok.   But this isn't very dramatic.  Far more compelling is this Hedychium, that was *completely* prevented from freezing by the very dense branches of a Taxodium 'Banita'.   The flowers still have their fragrance and everything.  They and the foliage are completely intact, even though they are in the lowest part of my garden.  Jewelweeds with a more open exposure, 20 ft away were completely killed.   Rather more amusingly, but not really having a positive benefit on the appearance of the garden, we see that even the large top leaves of a Brugmansia can 'shelter' the lower leaves!   It takes very little 'cover' to make a difference. What is going on?  On cold nights heat is radiated up toward the sky.  Even foliage that looks scant to our eyes can stop that radiation from happening.  That's the short explanation but let's delve into it a bit more. Let's first say that, we can also talk about overstory trees providing a form of protection not directly related to this heat blanketing effect.  For example, in much of the US, borderline rhododendrons and camellias will be hardier if there are evergreen tree branches above them simply because they will reduce the amountf ot dessicating winter sun that hits the foliage.  The is a long term effect taking place over weeks of winter, not an immediate effect happening during radiational freeze events. Where does overstory protection come into play?  In a garden like mine, it is *usually* simply prolonging the inevitable.   Which is still great, because I'd like to enjoy my ginger lilies for as long as possible.  I would say it makes the most dramatic difference in gardens that are still ridiculously mild by the standards of most of the CONUS. The most dramatic examples are not even going to be found on our continent, and possibly even our hemisphere.  Why?   Because there are 2 main types of freezes: radiative and advective.  Many freezes have a mixed characteristic, or can have an advective freeze on the first night and a radiative one the second night. However in a climate like Victoria, Australia, practically ALL of the freezes that could damage what they consider borderline vegetation are going to be radiative.  At least at all but the very highest elevations where few people live: more on that later.  There's simply no mechanism for an advective freeze of any magnitude to occur because there's so much Southern Ocean separating them from the very cold Antarctica.   If you watch the excellent videos of Stephen Ryan, patron of the Royal Horticultural Society of Victoria, you will see that overstory protection makes a HUGE difference in his garden on the slopes of Mt. Macedon.   He posts as \"The Horticulturalists\".   (my picture from 2016) The same theory applies, to varying degrees, to the rest of the world's maritime and/or subtropical climates.  Overstory protection is simply going to matter more for Seattle, than it does for Denver.   More for Atlanta than it does for Rye, NY.  But also, more for Sonoma County, CA, than Seattle.  However, almost anywhere in the US, except maybe somewhere like Catalina Island and Key West, CAN STILL HAVE DAMAGING ADVECTIVE FREEZES.   Simply because instead of a wide ocean separating us from Antarctica, we have Canada!  Thank you Canucks for nothing! (JK, srsly, this arrangement also benefits all of us by making the middle of the country a breadbasket and not a desert like AU)   This isn't to say that in a particular freeze in zn 5 Denver, overstory protection won't help prolong the season a bit, as they did in my zn 7 garden. Here's an example of that.  This Longan at the Jacksonville botanical garden was clearly planted with the idea that the huge live oaks would protect it from freezes. And in some winters, they probably did.  However the big freeze we had in the southeast last winter had a strong advective component, and you can see that it was still curtains for this truly tropical plant trying to grow in a \"continental subtropical climate\" (not \"maritime subtropical\", which is the taxonomic characterization I would devise for southeastern Australia)   Hope this gives you some food for thought and ideas for your garden planning, wherever you are!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/8a9204d40547e72e_1055-w500-h318-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/fc520e680547e72f_1102-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2ca221600547e730_1057-w500-h587-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/61d2516d0547e890_1408-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/1272127a0547e733_1103-w500-h330-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/16723dee0547e734_1103-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

main_question: {"author_id": "sheppardlake", "author_name": "sheppardlake", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/sheppardlake", "date": "2023-11-05", "text": "Hi pros! I am being charged for hours for each of these people plus 20% on top for the GC fees. Or is having someone different in these roles atypical? I want to be clear - I am not suggesting that the GC should not get their 20%. I'm just asking what is typical for each of these roles - and if it is typical to have all of these roles on one job. Thanks so much for your help!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "joseph-corlett-llc-pfvwus-pf~848525206", "author_name": "Joseph Corlett, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/general-contractors/joseph-corlett-llc-pfvwus-pf~848525206", "date": "2023-11-06", "text": "The GC is going to let you pay for as many of these people as you'll tolerate.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "charles-ross-homes-pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "author_name": "Charles Ross Homes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/design-build-firms/charles-ross-homes-pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "date": "2023-11-06", "text": "Asking your general contractor to cede control of your project to someone outside his company is a recipe for problems.  If you want to do it differently next time, that's fine.  Stay the course on this project and hold the GC accountable for the results.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "bry911", "author_name": "bry911", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bry911", "date": "2023-11-06", "text": "First, ignore typical percentages.  There are so many different contracts and payment terms that generalizations about percentages are not that valuable.  Look at what this is going to cost in total and see if it is within your budget and how that compares to other costs.  You shouldn't care if a contractor makes $100,000 or $40,000 if you pay the same either way.  So look at the price you are paying and the quality you are getting for that price, determine if that is comparable and reasonable then use that for the decision. The company I'm working with has connected me with an Interior Designer they use a lot. In addition, there is a separate project manager and a site supervisor. Those are quite literally why you hire a GC, and there is nothing wrong with the GC hiring people to assist him/her in doing those jobs, but there is a problem with a separate (hourly?) charge for their services and a bigger problem with a builder's percentage on top of that. Builds have two types of costs, direct costs and indirect costs.  Direct costs are those costs that go directly into producing the house such as the plumbing or electrical, so the entire plumbing or electrical bid would be a direct cost.  Indirect costs are those that are necessary for the house to get built but don't go directly into the house.  A builder's truck is a great example of an indirect cost.  Supervision is always indirect and that is what the builder's percentage is for... to cover overhead and profit.  Supervision of the work and the project management by the builder is overhead. Another way to think of this.  Suppose a builder can built two houses per year, making $40,000 profit from each one.  The builder decides to hire a site manager, which reduces the builder's profit off each home to $25,000 but allows the builder to build twice as many homes.  So instead of making $80,000 the builder is making $100,000 per year.  Suppose output can again double with a site manager... The builder might then only make $15,000 per home, but make it from 8 homes.  That is synergy and explains why a builder might want a site manager and project manager instead of doing all that work themselves. However, if the builder is charging the homeowner for that same project manager.  They are just increasing their profit from $80,000 ($40,000/home * 2 homes) to $172,000 (43,000/home * 4 homes). title: AGS and External Control questions for a Max-E-Therm 400 SR400NA heate | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "nick-shirley", "author_name": "nick_shirley", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nick-shirley", "date": "2023-11-06", "text": "Summary of questions about problems I\u2019m having with the heater today after trying to turn it on for the first time since March 2023: 1) Service Heater light turns on and AGS LED goes on before heater ignites. Just replace the automatic gas sensor plug or could other problems be causing this? 2) External control switch turns on the heater, but the display is still visible when the switch is turned to off when it\u2019s in Service Heater mode. Is this normal? Question 1: Starting the heater with a cold pool turns on the blower and the Heating light flashes. Within 15 seconds (but before the ignition fires), the Service Heater light comes on and Heating light turns off. About 5 seconds later while blower is still going, the Service Heater light goes out, the Heating light starts flashing again, and I get all excited at the idea the heater will work, but in about 15 seconds the SH light comes on and never goes out. Ignition never happens in this scenario, the blower eventually shuts off, and all is quiet. A check of the underside of the control board reveals the AGS error LED on. The heater is just three years old and the AGS plug is a very simple temperature sensor that would seem to be unlikely to fail in such a short time in operation, so that\u2019s unexpected. New plugs are cheap (about 30 bucks with tax) and easy to replace, but I\u2019m wondering if there\u2019s more going on even though the AGS light is the only lit error LED. Water flow is more than sufficient and water temps are about 78 degrees right now so it\u2019s not either of those problems. Any ideas of other areas to check out if the replacement sensor doesn\u2019t work? Question 2: I use an external three-way switch to launch the heater in either Pool or Spa mode (the \u201cmodes\u201d are actually just different target temp settings). In normal operation, (1) when the external control switch is Off, the membrane display is blank and no lights are on, (2) when the switch is turned to Pool or Spa the display is visible and the heater boot up begins and the appropriate lights are lit, and (3) when I turn off the switch so it\u2019s neither on Pool or Spa, the display blanks out. But when when I get the AGS error described in Question 1 , turning the switch to off doesn\u2019t blank out the display. It seems stuck as if it\u2019s permanently set to Pool or Spa. This is kind of handy when I\u2019m diagnosing the Question 1 issue because I can check the error lights, but it\u2019s weird because you\u2019d think turning the external switch to off would kill the display. Pushing membrane buttons seems to have no effect in this state. The only way I can return to the normal off behavior is to turn off all power to the heater and then restore the juice. The display is then blanked out as expected, but it\u2019ll go into the same frozen state once I turn the switch to Pool or Spa and the Service Heater light comes on. I\u2019m wondering if this is an intentional feature, so that if the heater detects any sort of serious error and lights the Service Heater LED, the user would be alerted to the issue even if the external control is set to Off (presumably fixing the problem would return the external control to normal operation). Use caution when asking for auto dial from a smart device Tell Alexa to play your favorite song. Ask Siri  about the weather. Use Google Assistant to turn down the air  conditioner. But don\u2019t ask your smart device to look up a phone number,  because it could accidentally point you to a scam. How the scam works: You  need the phone number for a company, so you ask your home\u2019s smart  device, which might be Google Home, Siri, or Alexa, to find and dial it  for you. But when the company\u2019s \u201crepresentative\u201d answers, you start to  notice some red flags. This representative may insist they can only help  you if you make a payment by wire transfer or prepaid debit cards.  Other times, they demand remote access to your computer or point you to a  scam website. One recent victim reported to BBB Scam Tracker: \u201cI  used Siri to look up the United Airlines customer service line.  Somehow, the call was connected to a different company\u2026 The agent  pretended to be a United Airlines agent and said he could help me cancel  my flight. The fee was $125. I was convinced it was United Airlines,  but the next day I realized my mistake. They said they would refund my  money, but only after I threatened to call the police. I\u2019m still waiting  for a refund.\u201d In another version of this  scam, a consumer tried using voice search to contact Roku with a  question about setting up their device. title: After the rains | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2023-11-06", "text": "Over the last two weeks or so we have gotten about seven inches of rain.  This may not sound like much to Americans, but it's more than we've received in the last several months put together, and is enough to matter.  We still need more, to replenish groundwater, fill the reservoir (which last I heard was still nearly empty), and keep everything watered, but this is a good start; I hope not the end.  I can hear the stream running down in the bottom of the valley.  Rain is forecast for Thursday night. As far as the garden goes, all is forgiven.  The last two days have been notably sunny and mild.  I have been fooling around in the big garden, not energetic enough for serious work, but doing a bit of much-needed pruning of the Italian cypresses, tidying beds of overgrown grass and weeds, and having my first look around in months.  The plants are looking greatly refreshed and pleased with themselves; the olives, cypresses, native oaks--deciduous, but still holding their mostly green leaves--the Mediterranean subshrubs, rosemary, Salvia greggii, phlomis, artemisia, are fine fettle, along with many others, and the winter annual grass is sprouting tender and fresh green.  Some losses:  one of my mature, beautiful plants of Daphne odora 'Aureomarginata' died--I think not due to drought--and of course all the 80-90 box are goners:  I've been cutting them down to the ground.  A number of previously non-prosperous roses are nearly, but not quite, dead.  Among the plants I put in the ground a year ago, the pomegranate, persimmon, and Viburnum tinus are dead, not to my surprise:  they were purchased plants put in poor ground (though pretty much all our ground is poor), both of which, perhaps, told against them.  On the other hand, the two purchased plants of Mahonia eurybracteata 'Soft Caress' held up egregiously!  Established shrubs for the most part did pretty well, as far as I've seen so far, including toughies like lilac, forsythia, photinia, winter honeysuckle.  Plants are tough!  They want to live! I was really pleased, and not entirely surprised, that many of the plants put in the ground a year ago are alive despite the long drought and very little watering, particularly the Mediterranean-climate subshrubs that I'm using more and more for hedging.  Phlomis, of which I have four or five varieties, I believe, is a champion.  Another favorite is shrub germander, Teucrium fruticans, a brilliantly silver subshrub, quite large, and handsome as can be.  I was wishing, when I saw my lentisk, that I knew where to get more young plants of it.  The current one, purchased when it was a baby, now covers a few square yards, very green, very vigorous, very handsome, with foliage that smells to me like Old Spice.  IT doesn't fear drought.  It's native further south; I don't think I've seen it grown locally, unfortunately.  I've had no luck propagating it. I'll have to get back on the roses.  The garden is turning more and more into a landscape garden, which isn't an evil fate, but I do want many roses, and many kinds of plants.  Including things like hardy cyclamen, one of the few things in bloom, and a delight of the season.  They're late this year, currently in full flower, and cute as they can be. I would like to hear from Bart, having been wondering about the weather where she is.  There was flooding in her part of Italy.", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "mxk3", "author_name": "porkchop_z5b_MI", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mxk3", "date": "2023-11-07", "text": "What is this induction \"learning curve\" people have mentioned?  I've seen it cited numerous times on the board but don't recall it actually being explained.  I get that you have to learn the appliance itself (i.e. read the manual), but outside of that, why does one need to learn how to use induction?    Turn up the heat, turn down the heat, it's responsive -- same as gas, right?  Can someone please explain this to me? I'm going to the Wolf showroom today for a demo (actual food!), want to have a discussion w/DH about it on the trip over, since he's the one that will actually be doing the cooking during the demo (fun!)", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2023-11-07", "text": "Perhaps the most important retraining aspect is setting a power level to bring something to a boil quickly, intending to later turn the power down, and then walking away \"for a moment.\"  You will find that most induction hobs are capable of more power transfer to the pan/pot than similarly sized gas burners.  So the retraining is to not walk away until you have a firm sense of timing for the power level vs. pot contents, or can accurately set a timer to alarm before you have a mess. I have a small RevereWare pot that I boil eggs in.  On my smallest burner this takes 2 minutes at power boost.  The time between incipient boiling (some visible bubbles at the pot base and no noise) and hot water splashing over the cooktop and counter is less than 20 seconds.  I use a timer and don't leave the kitchen, even briefly, until (a) boiling has been reached, (b) I have turned the power level down to a known value for steady-state boiling mode, and (c) set the timer for the desired boiling time.", "images": []}}

I've been highly nearsighted my whole life, so chose to have near-distance (-2) monofocal lenses implanted since my ophthalmologist, who was also my surgeon, suggested I would be happier with what my brain was already used to, i.e. being able to read, which I do a lot of, without glasses. Oedema Oedema (aka edema) is a physiological disorder that can affect all terrestrial plants. It occurs when the plant takes up more water than it can rid itself of via the process of transpiration. Symptoms are seen more frequently in plants that are fleshy, are usually more pronounced on the underside of leaves, and older/lower leaves are more likely to be affected than younger/upper leaves. Oedema is most common in houseplants during the winter/early spring months, is driven primarily by excessive water retention in the soil, and can be intensified via several additional cultural influences. main_question: {"author_id": "shuchi-mishra100", "author_name": "Plant Girl", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/shuchi-mishra100", "date": "2023-11-08", "text": "Hello Community, Zone: 10b (Los Angeles, CA) We recently transplanted 10-12 feet Magnolia Champaca tree (also called Michelia Champaca/Himalayan Champaca) to different spot in ground. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "floral-uk", "author_name": "floral_uk z.8/9 SW UK", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/floral-uk", "date": "2023-11-08", "text": "Oh dear.  I would not hold out too much hope for this poor tree.  Firstly, these resent being transplanted however careful you are. Magnolias and their relations have big fleshy roots rather than many fibrous roots and they are slow to regrow. If the roots were not conserved it's going to be even less happy. Secondly, cutting most of its branches off was an unfortunate move.  It is a long held gardening myth that reducing top growth promotes root development. Sadly, it doesn't. It forces the tree try to make replacement top growth from dormant buds, not roots.  Transplanting - Should You Reduce Top Growth? (gardenmyths.com) But it's done now. title: Brown is back!? Whaaat? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mtnrdredux-gw", "author_name": "mtnrdredux_gw", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mtnrdredux-gw", "date": "2023-11-09", "text": "Real Simple, 6 Kitchen Cabinet Trends You\u2019ll See in 2024 One huge trend we\u2019re seeing across the board in design is the color brown and anything brown-adjacent, especially woods. Going overboard with wood in rooms by way of wall paneling and layering large furniture pieces of different species is especially in vogue because it adds an intense organic warmth and texture. Speaking of warm colors, red and orange undertones are slowly creeping into wood kitchen cabinets. (This is in addition to the light wood grains we mentioned earlier.) It\u2019s a trend that makes sense from a design perspective\u2014earthy paint shades like clay and terracotta have been the buzz for a few years now so it\u2019s natural for those reddish hues to spill into other materials. MasterBrand says, \u201cHues of warm orange-reds are showing up on walls, furnishings, and decor, adding depth and character to interiors and providing a visual focal point that effortlessly draws the eye in and sparks interest without taking away from a neutral, earthy space.\u201d ElleDecor 2024 Kitchen trends, These 2024 Kitchen Trends Are Already Coming in Hot Mixing light or dark-stained woods in with saturated colors also is big. \u201cI think a balance of painted and wood cabinetry is really important,\u201d says Macuga. \u201cColor can provide a space with personality and charm, and stained woods give a space a feeling of warmth and depth.\u201d   Hello, pendulum. The thing that always gets me is the tone in these pieces. Whatever happens to be in vogue, they give a reason and that's that. They make it sound as if there is no other way to look at it. So when all white kitchens were it, we were told that it was timeless, sanitary, and light-filled and that was why it was the right choice, period. Something else comes in style, and then they go back and deride white as cold and boring. But at the time no one writes what they should, which would be \"No style is timeless, but white K are popular among those who want to maximize light and like utilitarian K and BA spaces, even though some whites are cold and some prefer more color in their spaces.\"", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/fa423d8f054cc7ca_0700-w500-h362-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Help with contradictions between vendor and glass mfgr on Low E 366 | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "candlernc", "author_name": "Kris McClure", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/candlernc", "date": "2023-11-10", "text": "We had two sets of sliders installed with Jeld-Wen Sun Resist tempered glass (told to be the same as Low E 366) with two additional stationary panels (approx 3 x 7 feet each) between the sliders.  Sliders are perfect, but the two panels of glass, which the attached paper stickers said \"1/8\" Cardinal 366 Tempered\" glass have a horrible bronze color when the sun shines on them in the mornings.  Once the sun is gone, they look no different from the Jeld-Wen glass.  They have been replaced once already, reversed in case they were put in backwards, but still no change.  Now the vendor they were purchased from has said they were \"done\" and after contacting Cardinal Glass first and being told that they manufactured glass but AIG actually assembled the product for distribution,  we still haven't gotten anywhere as AIG says \"that's the way it is\".  Most issues we've read address a possible \"green\" tint, but these are very significantly bronze.  The label on the glass reads: AIG Tempered ANSI Z97 1 - 2015 16CFR 1201-II SGCC 3859 1/8UA We really don't know what to do at this point, but we feel they are definitely not right and no one will accept responsibility.  We've been fighting this for over a year.  Can any window installer/sales rep/distributor/etc. give us an honest opinion and suggestion on what to do?  Many thanks!!!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/7192857c054e85de_4908-w500-h500-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "oberon476", "author_name": "oberon476", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/oberon476", "date": "2023-11-13", "text": "If I was visiting your home to investigate the glass in the doors, this is one of the devices that I would have with me. https://www.edtm.com/field-service-tools/other-field-service-tools/wp4500-window-energy-profiler The first number used in the Cardinal coating designations stands for the number of silver layers in the coating, and the next two numbers are the visible light transmittance. I want good CFM and I also want high quality CRI with the lighting. I'm attracted to the contemporary \"T\" shaped ones. Tell me about your horrible vent and why I should avoid yours.. What are the good brands?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/6772e1a0054f1810_2321-w500-h689-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2023-11-11", "text": "With induction, there are no gas combustion products, but the food being cooked is being cooked at the same temperatures with the same cooking plume generation.  Plumes can have fairly high upward velocities, and hence momenta, such that when plume portions meet the hood structures some may reflect downward.  One wants to entrain all of it in the flow through the baffles. Further, the plumes diverge from their points of generation, making the plume volume look like an upside down ice cream cone, with the point somewhere below the pan.  Divergence may vary with whether gas or induction, but is unlikely to be narrower than ten degrees from vertical around the pan edge.  And this angle is for the highest velocity components.  Without air movement, weak but still wet and greasy plume 'rays' diverge at wider angles, but due to lower momentum are entrained in the hood air flow if the flow is high enough. For a given energetic cooking project, one can argue that the total CFM needed to keep the velocity adequate at the baffles can be lower with induction, but this is very dependent on total plume CFM and how much averaging is performed in the reservoir area below the baffles.  Huge reservoirs used in commercial hoods (extending from 7 ft to 10 ft high) perform nearly full averaging of plumes over the baffle space, and thereby allow lower CFM for a given cooking project, at least to the point where the total plume CFM from all plumes approaches the hood CFM. Insight into this topic may be found in the 'Greenheck Guide' available here: https://www.tagengineering.ca/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/KVSApplDesign_catalog.pdf The first dozen of so pages should be sufficient.", "images": []}}

title: How big should a lamp be on a table | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "vintagelite-pfvwgb-pf~382206980", "author_name": "VINTAGELITE", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/appliances/vintagelite-pfvwgb-pf~382206980", "date": "2023-11-11", "text": "Selecting the appropriate size for a table lamp involves considering several factors to ensure it complements the table and the surrounding space. The size of the lamp should be proportional to the table and its intended purpose. If the table is small, opt for a more petite lamp to maintain balance and prevent it from overwhelming the space. Conversely, larger tables can accommodate more substantial lamps that make a bold statement. The height of the table lamp is crucial in achieving the right visual impact. The bottom of the lampshade should ideally be at eye level when seated, ensuring optimal lighting for reading or other activities. For bedside tables, the lamp's height should align with the top of the mattress.   Additionally, consider the lampshade diameter. A general guideline is that the diameter should be approximately half the width of the table. This helps distribute light evenly and prevents the lampshade from appearing disproportionate to the table. The overall design aesthetic of the room and the table itself should also influence your choice. A modern, minimalist table may benefit from a sleek and streamlined lamp, while a more ornate table could pair well with a lamp featuring intricate details.   Ultimately, personal preference plays a significant role. If the lamp resonates with your style and contributes to the desired atmosphere, it's likely the right fit. Experimenting with different sizes and styles allows you to find the perfect balance, ensuring that the table lamp not only illuminates the space effectively but also enhances the overall aesthetics of the room.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5da2a92b054f5df4_0213-w500-h500-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/d6e28648054f5df5_0215-w500-h500-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/0c9299a1054f5df7_0216-w500-h500-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

I made the video and contacted Ekornes with it. Ekornes told dealer to give full refund, we will cover it. title: Before & After Kitchen refresh: Blue Skies! (note: many pix!) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lp2020", "author_name": "Leslie P", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lp2020", "date": "2023-11-11", "text": "Greetings! Wanted to post to thank the Houzz community for insights and advice as I\u2019ve been working on refreshing the kitchen. My original post (link below) asked questions around a quartzite countertop , and I got a lot of feedback and food for thought and rethinking. Cristallo Blue as Countertop - is bleeding inevitable? It\u2019s been quite the journey, but as of today I\u2019m happy to report that we\u2019ve finished the basic refresh of the space. Have not yet finished the repopulation, but I\u2019m just glad we got through this stage! Sharing some of the story and photos that they may provide thoughts for others with unique design challenges; also submitting as proof that the kitchen was clean at least once \ud83d\ude0a  Sorry the post is so long, but didn't want to miss anything;  and I find that the completion has brought genuine smiles and a sense of happiness that, for me, has been sorely missing for some time.  So, here we go.... Before: standard suburban kitchen, late 90s construction, honey oak abounds.  Dinette area attached, with sliding door that opens to the deck, open connection to the family room on the non-kitchen side. Original cabinetry; we added the hardware a couple years in.   Main kitchen area.  30 inch upper cabinets, no backsplash aside from the 4\" attached to the countertop.  The stove and microwave were about a week old when this picture was taken late last year; you can clearly see the outlines of the amateur paint job where our old stove used to be :)  Pantry area (drywall enclosed, wire shelving inside ) and side drawer below.  Opening to the formal dining room is to the right, main hallway is to the left.   Sink area: original dual basin sink, double hung window and flush-mount light.   And now, After: The Ceiling is the Star, the other elements support it. Hadn't planned to originally go all-white on the cabinetry, but that's where we ended up.  Purposefully sought elements with cooler undertones - if I'd put warmer tones on the cabinets,  they likely would have read yellow against the clouds and sky. We cut the soffits back, which allowed us to expand the upper cabinets to 36 inches high (ceilings are standard 8 ft).  Really helped to give a sense or space and 'air-y' ness.   Pantry and microwave area below.  Reconfigured the space a bit to get rid of the drywall 'wall', and replace it with an actual pantry cabinet. The removal gave us about 4 inches of extra space  (you can see vestiges of where it was on the reduced soffit above), and that plus another inch or so gave us a new home for the OTR microwave - it's not yet a year old, has all the features I want on it (finally!), works great, and for holidays, it is my second oven - couldn't part with it.  It doesn't know it's not above a range..... but we mounted it similarly.  The light now works great to illuminate the 'drop zone' below it.   Pantry interior - Yay, no more wire shelves!  This was a custom configuration with the cabinet manufacturer; glad I was workign with a kitchen designer to help convey what I was looking for.  I'm not a fan of pull-outs; went older-school instead, strongly inspired by British larder/pantry cabinets.  The door shelves help to maximize use of the space, and the cut-back interior shelves keep them from getting too deep.   The difference in door cabinet depths is intentional.  Will be adding lighting to the interior.   Fridge and stove wall:  happy to have a true vent hood that vents outside.  Found one that goes farther over the stove than the microwave did, so there's a chance to catch effluent from the front burners.  Couldn't see doing open shelves on the upper surfaces;  too much dust and grease accumulation.   And, finally added actual backsplash; kept in the blue/white color scheme, but had fun adding a feeling of moving water with the textured tile behind the hood.  Trying to reduce clutter on the counters, looking forward to using this pull-out to keep utensils and knives close by, but out of sight.  The vertical board storage will (hopefully) help remove a long-standing source of frustration, trying to search in a horizontal stack for the desired one.  (and, it will help with decluttering - only so many will fit in there).     Sink wall:  new sink, new faucet (the one countertop seam in the kitchen is where the faucet hole is), swapped out the dual-hung window for one that was slightly longer, and casement style.  Replaced flush mount light;  my one ode to recessed lighting in the whole kitchen is here - flush with the reduced soffit, a flat pancake-like LED assembly thingie.  Gives great light for the space configuration; I can work there without casting shadows.     And, I'm a long-time dual-basin sink person; but will have to give props to the Houzz community for convincing me to try a single basin sink .  I'm liking it more than I thought I would - so much more space!  And I have a smaller bin under the sink if I feel a need to run a smaller basin of washwater for something.    The Island.... The KD was really helpful in giving us ideas to reimagine this a  but: coordinating color, going with stained vs. painted for some textural contrast.  Trash bin pullouts on the right side.  One purposeful addition of a cabinet here, for a couple of appliances that will go on pullouts. We had an outlet on the previous island (it was on the end, which I didn't like) and needed one here for code regulations. Thankful that the KD had a good suggestion for how to utilize the space underneath it;  rather than be filler, it houses a small stepstool - so I have one close by, and I'm able to actually reach the tops of those new higher upper cabinets!   The lighting.  This took some thinking:  putting in the standard kitchen recessed lighting would have resulted in seriously disrupting the Sky Ceiling, which was a non-starter; and I'm really not a fan of recessed lighting in any event.   Instead, we opted to go with a track pendant configuration - utilized the one junction box available, configured track to center over the island, raise it a bit (since it's being used as general lighting here more than task lighting), and add some higher watt-equivalent LEDs to brighten it up.  With three of them, it really lights up the space well - a lot of light reflects off of the ceiling and cabinets; and combined with the under cabinet lighting added in, the layers fill in any spots that would have been dark/shady.  The shade glass gives a greenish tint when they're off, but it still blends pretty well with the other colors.     And last, the dinette area.  The current table and chairs will be replaced.  Overhead lighting keeps in sync with the motion/round theme.  Had a major case of decision fatigue by the time it came to select a window treatment for the sliding door - needed something that would be easy to open, give a bit of light filtering during the day, but some privacy at night as our neighbors aren't far away.  Sheer shades seemed to fit the bill for that; they were on sale; and they came in white - decision made :)   Didn't think we'd be done before Thanksgiving, but here we are! other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "dchall-san_antonio", "author_name": "dchall_san_antonio", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dchall-san_antonio", "date": "2023-11-13", "text": "Rossmoor/Los Alamitos is so helpful.  My college roommate lives just south of Edinger, so I have some familiarity with the area and microclimate.  He has been successful with a fescue lawn for 30 years or so.  Unlike most of SoCal, he tries to water once a week.  Also he mows at his mower's highest setting, and it looks pretty good all the time.  Even on satellite pictures, his is among the greenest lawns.  You might be in the realm that can get away with a fescue like Marathon I, II, or III.  Those are slow growing and considered to be dwarf, but if you let them get tall, they look better (to me). As for leveling the ground, you have to do that first.  If you are redoing the entire lawn it is much easier to do the leveling.  Here's the basic plan.  Kill the lawn with RoundUp or whatever you prefer.  Then determine if you already have too much soil.  I'm going to suggest that most people have too much soil, and at that point, this becomes a job for a professional landscaper.  If you happen to have just enough soil, then look for high spots and low spots.  You can tell by walking on it, but you can tell a lot more by rolling a lawn mower over it.  If the wheels of the mower bump along, then you have something to work with.  If they roll smoothly, then you're good to go.  If you have a bumpy lawn, then get lots of bags of leveling sand.  I really like the paver leveling sand found in the nursery department of Home Depot.  It is relatively coarse compared to fine sands you see in the masonry department.  Being coarse will help the sand to interlock and not shift around like beach sand.  Dump the sand out and get started leveling with a rake.  Once you have it more or less spread out, then use a drag to really smooth out the surface.  Here is a picture of a drag you can buy, but basically it's chain link fencing and a 2x4 keeping it spread apart.   It will need some weight on it to hold it down.  Drag the drag around and add sand to the low spots as you see fit.  Once you think it's perfect, then water it to help settle the sand.  You will see new low spots appear as the water works through the sand.  Add more sand to the low spots and drag some more.  Then water, settle, and look for low spots.  Usually 3 times is enough to get it perfect.  You might see some spots where the original soil shows through.  This is fine.  After the last watering, it's time for seed.  Scatter the seed according to the directions on the bag or box of seed.  After the seed it is time to roll the seed down into the surface of the sand. Note that I did not mention rototilling.  Rototilling is the single most important reason why most bumpy lawns are bumpy.  A manual rototiller cannot be controlled well enough to get a perfectly \"level\" depth of tillage.  The result is the soil will settle unevenly the very first day after tilling and get worse for the next 3 years. I've probably raised many questions. I learned something valuable.  I had to dig out 3 roses along an old fence that was being replaced.  They had been there at least 15 years.  When we started digging them out, it was shocking [although it shouldn't have been] at how compacted the soil was and how full of tree roots it was.  We managed to get two roses out with an intact rootball and pot them up to wait to be replanted.  The third rose was right up against a post of the fence and it was a New Dawn, that is a very vigorous rose.  First attempt at moving one.  The root system on that was amazing, how deep it went.  We tried to get a rootball out but in the end we had to just cut it out of the ground basically.  I was convinced that we had killed it and it didn't have enough roots to survive, and we threw it away. The next day, I was looking at photos of the work and saw the stump of a rose as we took it out of the ground and I thought, oh wow, that might have been okay if I planted it in a pot with some good soil and took care of it for a couple of weeks. About 3 weeks later, I was ready to replant the other two roses we had dug out with roots and they had already developed a lot of new, white beautiful roots!  And really, they did have a small rootball, but they also had these long bare branches that had a few leaves at the end, because the rabbits had eaten the lower foliage in the spring.  I left about 8 of these 3ft long canes on each rose despite so few leaves and I really didn't think they were going to make it either. So that is the lesson I learned. Preciso che la casa \u00e8 abbastanza secca (55-62% di umidit\u00e0) e tengo l'umidit\u00e0 monitorata in prossimit\u00e0 del portone in pi\u00f9 punti. A cosa pu\u00f2 essere dovuto il problema? Come posso risolvere?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~597310718", "author_name": "Caterina Martini", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~597310718", "date": "2023-11-30", "text": "si tratta di un ponte termico. Differenza di temperatura tra la parete e il punto di raccordo tra portoncino e muro. Se il portoncino rispetta i parametri di legge in tema di isolamento termico e se ci\u00f2 che ti hanno venduto corrisponde alla scheda tecnica del prodotto (e ritengo entrambe le condizioni estremamente probabili), l'azienda non pu\u00f2 fare assolutamente nulla. title: Pie crust mishap - possibly fortunate? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "publickman", "author_name": "Lars", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/publickman", "date": "2023-11-13", "text": "We had neighbors over for a barbecue yesterday (Sunday), and I started preparing food the day before (Saturday), although I probably should have started on Friday. I was going to make pie crust on Friday and noticed I did not have shortening, but rather than go to the store, I ordered some from Amazon, and it arrived around 6 PM on Saturday, which did give me time to make the pie crust that evening, which I did. I used the recipe that I normally use, but that recipe is for two 2-crust pies, and I only wanted to make one.  The crust recipe calls for one egg, and so I looked up the weight of one egg, divided it in half and came up with 0.82 oz for half of an egg, so that I could weigh it out. The method of the crust calls for mixing part of the flour (I used 1/2 cup WW and 1 cup AP, to start), 1/2 tsp salt, and 1 Tbsp sugar in the food processor.  Then add 1/2 cup chilled shortening, cut into small pieces (I did this with a small spoon) and 3/4 cup (1-1/2 sticks) chilled butter, also in small pieces. I had stored a stick of butter in the freezer, uncut, but I had taken the 1/2 stick and cut into small pieces and stored it in the freezer with the pieces of shortening in a small bowl.  When I took the bowl of shortening and butter out to add to the FP, I forgot to take out the whole stick of butter, and proceeded with the recipe and processed with shortening and 1/4 cup butter. After the butter and first addition of flour had been processed for 10 seconds, I added another cup of AP flour and pulsed 4-6 times.  The dough looked pretty much the way it was supposed to according to the recipe, at first like cottage cheese, and then after the rest of the flour, it was more like cornmeal. I moved the mixture to a large bowl and added the chilled liquid (1/6 cup vodka, 1/2 egg, and 1/6 cup water - adjusted to make 1/2 cup total) and folded the dough to make it come together.  It was a bit dry, and so I spritzed it with water to make it come together, and then I divided it into two flat discs, wrapped those in plastic wrap, and stored them in the refrigerator. About half an hour later, I happened to notice that the stick of butter that I was supposed to use was still in the freezer, and I panicked a bit.  Then I decided that I was somehow going to get the butter into the dough. I took one piece of dough out and broke it into pieces into the bowl that I had used for mixing it.  Then I cut the stick of butter in half and grated it and added that to the bowl and tried to stir this together.  I ended up using my hands to fold the butter into the dough, but the butter remained in pieces the size that it was when it came out of the grater.  I decided that this was good and formed the dough back into a disc and put it back in the fridge.  Then I did the same with the other disc, and I left them in the fridge overnight. The next morning I baked the focaccia dough that I had made the day before, and while that was baking, I made the filling for the apple pie. The pie crust rolled out very easily, and the shreds of butter were very visible in the dough.  This reminded me of a pie crust recipe that I had seen on ATK in which I think they had used a similar method of mixing the dough as I had accidentally done.  The pie came out probably better than what I had made before, but now I am wondering what I should learn from this accident.   The giraffe head is another accident.  Incidentally, while I was making the filling, I decided to add a couple of tablespoons of powdered fruit pectin - just because I had it and had not been using it.  I bought it thinking it would help with my arthritis - it does not - only the liquid fruit pectin works for me for that. title: What watt light bulb for living room | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "vintagelite-pfvwgb-pf~382206980", "author_name": "VINTAGELITE", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/appliances/vintagelite-pfvwgb-pf~382206980", "date": "2023-11-14", "text": "Wattage for light bulbs in your living room is a nuanced process that involves considering various factors to create the desired ambiance and functionality. The living room serves as a multifunctional space, accommodating activities from relaxation and entertainment to socializing. The size of the room plays a crucial role in determining the suitable wattage for lighting fixtures. For overhead fixtures like chandeliers or ceiling-mounted lights, a wattage range of 60 to 100 watts per bulb is often recommended. title: Finished at last! Kitchen reno using Ikea, IKD, and Scherr's | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "vicki-mm", "author_name": "VLM", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/vicki-mm", "date": "2023-11-15", "text": "Recently completed our kitchen reno and wanted to share our experience with Ikea Sektion cabinets, Scherr\u2019s fronts, and IKD (Inspired Kitchen Design) design help, in case anyone finds the info useful. SPECIFICS ON RENO: Where:  Orange Cty, CA When:  Apr, 2023 Why:  Home built in 1972 and kitchen was original! How much:  Cabinets, installed, approx. $19k, cost of entire reno, w/ appliances, $35k. We kept original oak flooring (for now). After 30+ years in our home, and sending 3 kids off to college, we finally got around to a much-needed kitchen remodel. The reno was largely DIY, but we hired an electrician, IKD, and had a guy help with the cabinet install. Along with invaluable input from Houzzers, both Scherr\u2019s and IKD offered plenty of answers when I needed them. We had 3 estimates of $38+k for basic cabinets alone with full-service cabinet companies and I still would\u2019ve been limited to specific sizes. Complete custom was even more. Our 13x16 kitchen is small -- with two corners and a peninsula, all design challenges! Orig (ideal) plan was to change the layout, remove peninsula and add an island, which was cost-prohibitive once we got estimates ($100k). This was our compromise and now that it\u2019s done, it was so worth it! Can\u2019t believe we lived with that 4\u201d tile countertop & \u00bd\u201d grout for 30 years! ******IKEA****** We modified 8 of our 21 cabinets. We modified in width, height, and depth. Height was easiest, then width, then depth. It def got easier as it went along, but in retrospect, I\u2019d consider paying for the modifications to depth, especially if you\u2019re using a company to install who is familiar w/ Ikea. The quotes we rec\u2019d for mods to cabs were very reasonable ($40-$50/cabinet). We did this so we could make the most use of the space. We ended up with two 5\u201d tray/wine storage cabs and one 3\u201d pullout. Also three 10\u201d deep on back side of peninsula for more storage. (in place of former bar seating since it was never used that way.). We also extended the height of oven and refrigerator top cabinets by a couple inches (so they actually go up higher on inside than crown moulding on outside reveals) by ordering a larger size and cutting down. That's the benefit of ordering separate fronts and not using Ikea's. You get to order your doors/drawers in ANY size! I utilized Ikea\u2019s design services and found them useful, though IKD was much more thorough. But having a contact with Ikea at the Design Center enabled me to call & email the same person when checking on product availability. Our reno was done Feb-Apr 2023, and most everything was available. We had to wait for a couple cabinet sizes and a couple other items, but really not much. I did do my share of driving to each of the four Ikea\u2019s within an hour of us though. VERY pleased with the quality of the cabinets. We were always, always, always going to install ourselves. We thought why go this route if you don't DIY? But honestly, there was a lot going on in our lives and it came down to TIME. We did the mods to the cabs, but used a guy I met in a cabinet shop near me to install. He had his own business and ended up spending about 7 full days on the job, which included crown. This was close to a $4k expense we didn't plan on, but ... we also were prepared for unexpected expenses. It seems they're part of every remodel. This was one. The biggest. We were actually quite happy with his work and attention to detail. As for the cabinets, they're very sturdy. He used plywood plinths so I can\u2019t speak to the plastic Sektion legs, but everything is super stable and level. Love the flexibility of shelf heights, drawer inserts. One thing I did NOT like was the vertical adjustments of the drawers. Almost useless, and have read many reports of others feeling same. Otherwise, the drawers are wonderful. Cooktop cab \u2013 It\u2019s 10-10-10 and we were able to put a hidden drawer directly under the Bosch induction cooktop. This gives us ENORMOUS storage for all those space-hogging utensils. We ended up with 1\u201d plywood subtop on the cabs (long story) which made this easier. We used four hidden drawers. LOVE, LOVE, LOVE them. If space is tight, they make all the difference. ******IKD****** Definitely worth the cost ($400). They are super familiar with any & all things Ikea, so they had every answer to my questions. I also found them responsive to my fairly frequent emails. The designs they supplied even detailed the modifications we needed to each cabinet so it was a useful resource we (and our cab installer) referred to often. Trust me, I spent f-o-r-e-v-e-r researching everything, and I still benefitted from their service. Can you do it without them? Yes. Do I wish I had? No. ******SCHERRS****** I worked extensively with Brandy, though Travis was involved off and on. Both were wonderful! I feel like I had hours of phone conversations with Brandy, plus countless emails, since we covered every detail in length. They noticed things I wouldn\u2019t have caught\u2026like making sure we ordered the peninsula end panel longer if we wanted it to extend to the floor, hinge locations, stain colors, etc. Travis had a sample made of the stain I wanted with three different finish options and sent them so I wouldn\u2019t be ordering blind. The quality of the doors/drawers is amazing. And expensive. $12k. Considering the cabinets were about $3k, it was a huge part of the entire kitchen remodel cost. But, it\u2019s also arguably the most noticeable, so I don\u2019t regret it at all. ******APPLIANCES****** Refrigerator \u2013 Bosch 800 Series 20.5 cu ft 4-door French Door counter depth smart refrigerator. Model B36CL80ENS/08 Purchased at Best Buy (\u201cOpen Box, new condition\u201d). Dishwasher \u2013 Miele G 7166 SCVi Auto Dos (this DW is amazing \u2013 you don\u2019t even have to add detergent if using their discs that automatically add it. It can also be controlled with wifi.) We had originally wanted Bosch 800 Series but it was impossible to find in stock. Miele had comparable ratings and it was similar in price, and had what we felt were even more features. Purchased at Pirch, Costa Mesa. Cooktop \u2013 Bosch Benchmark 30\u201d Induction Cooktop NITP060SUC. Purchased at Home Depot. Undercounter Beverage Center \u2013 GE Caf\u00e9 Smart Platinum Glass Model CCR06BM2PS5. This was a difficult purchase \u2013 it was more than the refrigerator! I went back and forth in rationalizing it. Biggest reason we chose it was it\u2019s flush installation and integrated handle. It\u2019s in full view when you first see the kitchen so installation mattered. We also needed it close to door so the flush handle was perfect. Tons of other features also. Purchased at Home Depot. Ceiling Vent Hood - Faber High-Light Ceiling Flush Mount Hood in white matte. Model HILTIS36WHNB This was another difficult purchase. But we lived in this home for 30 years with only a downdraft vent that vented into the cabinet below! So we knew we wanted a better ventilation system but it was over a peninsula that sat between the family room and backyard. With a pool. We did not want to block the view. This was a perfect solution and although very pricey ($3k with separate blower and another $2,500 for installation by an HVAC company) I am very VERY happy we chose it. Purchased at RSSA in Anaheim after speaking with Faber\u2019s rep and having him authorize RSSA to meet another dealer\u2019s online price. Sink \u2013 Ruvati 33\u201d Workstation Double Ledge Model RVH8222. This was the closest I could find to the Galley Workstation sink I wanted (but couldn\u2019t justify the cost?) Purchased at Home Depot Faucet \u2013 Delta Marca single handle pull-down sprayer Model 19780Z SD-DST Purchased at Lowe\u2019s. Important note \u2013 we installed the handle facing front to minimize water on counter. Love the way it works! Automatic Soap Dispenser\u2013 MAC Faucets electronic, sensor liquid soap dispenser model PYOS-1100. This was something I searched for forever. Needed a dispenser in brushed nickel with a long reach so it would extend PAST the ledges in sink. The one that came with the sink was the standard 3.5\u201d reach so soap would just fall right on the edge of the sink ledge. Love that this one is automatic. Even comes with remote to control amount dispensed and sensor range. Purchased from Electronic Faucets in Paramount, CA. Oven \u2013 GE Caf\u00e9 Double Oven \u2013 we bought it 7 years ago and was the only thing we kept from our old kitchen. We love it. IKD asked me what advice I\u2019d have for others and my reply was this: Don\u2019t be afraid. When it comes to Ikea, there is zero shortage of people who have done whatever you are going to do. There will be blogs, videos, Houzz and Reddit forums, and unlimited Instagram accounts for you to follow. I messaged people all over the world in the course of our kitchen remodel and found just about everyone was more than willing to answer questions. IKD was a great resource for the cost of their service. Well worth it. For us, it was just one important piece of the whole kitchen puzzle, which is made up of many, many pieces. As first-time kitchen remodelers, we wanted as much help putting that puzzle together as possible. Probably my biggest piece of advice is RESEARCH, RESEARCH, RESEARCH. It\u2019s time consuming but consider it time well-spent if it saves you money on making expensive mistakes you may have to either live with, or fix later. Also, once it\u2019s done, it\u2019s DONE, and you get to enjoy all your effort every day! Below are some before/after photos. Long story short, after a few years the osb expanded, which wasn't a problem as far as how it was installed because we left 1/8-1/4 gaps.  The challenge is that when we went back to remove and complete the rest of the flooring the osb had expanded upward about 3/16 so the new boards which are about 9/16 don't line up very well. The challenge I'm faced with is the new osb fitting the old and I'm wondering if I need to tear it all out or if there's a way to salvage what I have. title: Shopping the resell shop on half price day | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jehanne-hansen", "author_name": "claudia valentine", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jehanne-hansen", "date": "2023-11-16", "text": "Every Wednesday the local SA store has half price on clothing.   I used to do a lot of thrift shopping some years ago, but not so much in the last few years. I started going in on half price day just for amusment and I have bought a handful of better quality things that I found.   But, only a few. Yesterday as I was waiting in the long line for couple of things, and wondering if the couple of bucks difference was worth the long line, I began to talk to others around me .   Both the lady in front and the lady in back of me  were buying clothes to resell on a website called \"poshmark\". One lady gushed over the couple of itmes that she claimed were originally selling for a high price when new and she was looking up the current resell value on a refernce site. I asked her what she hoped to sell it for and it was a high price, also. The lady behind me was a young lady and she had a big bag like an Ikea bag that was full.  She was doing the same thing!   I saw her going through the racks with an efficient and targeted attention so that she flipped through them very quickly and she covered a rack full in short order!  She knew exactly what she was looking for.  She also was reselling. It is not as if they are doing something illegal or unethical.  They have only as much opportunity to buy these things from the store as does anyone else. One lady said that she was not so much in it for the profit, but she loved doing it.  The other lady was a bit less forthcoming. I have heard critical talk of the people who do this.  Some say that they are unfairly skimming the cream from the top.   But, all they are doing is shopping just like anyone else.   I think that maybe the one lady thought that I might be negative about it and did not want to be in a position to have to  defend herself and that is why she was not as willing to talk about it.    But, I dont care.   But. the other lady was glad to tall about what she was doing, and I was genuinely curious . This is not the first time that I have encountered people doing this.  The last time I was in line there was a lady who had found an expensive coat and was checking the resell value online and she was going to send it to her daughter who resells these things. If I have encountered so much of this in my visits to the store, there mush be quite a few doing this. There must be, at any given moment, someone in that line who is planning on reselling.
