title: just moved my zone | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2023-11-17", "text": "Well, I used to be in USDA plant hardiness zone 8b. Climate change has now moved me to 9a. Need to change my Houzz header! Check out the new plant hardiness zone maps. Though we've had a couple of zone 6-7 winter episodes in the last few years. https://planthardiness.ars.usda.gov/ Be aware that these zone maps are only about how severely cold your winter is. They have absolutely nothing to do with summer climate heat. I'm in the same zone now as what I used to have when I lived in the PNW, and my summer climate now is NOTHING like what I used to have there.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "theforgottenone1013", "author_name": "theforgottenone1013 (SE MI zone 5b/6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/theforgottenone1013", "date": "2023-11-18", "text": "Per the ARS/USDA site regarding the updated 2023 map:\"Plant hardiness zone designations represent what\u2019s known as the \u201caverage annual extreme minimum temperature\u201d at a given location during a particular time period (30 years, in this instance). Put another way, the designations do not reflect the coldest it has ever been or ever will be at a specific location, but simply the average lowest winter temperature for the location over a specified time. Low temperature during the winter is a crucial factor in the survival of plants at specific locations.\"My initial comment about playing it safe is further reinforced by this info. I knew it was about average minimum temperatures, not necessarily the coldest it has ever gotten in a location, but I think that bumping almost everyone up half a zone or more knowing that it can get colder in their location (and has done so very recently) may be a bit irresponsible. And I don't know how they can use the word \"thrive\" the way they do (used elsewhere on their site, as Dan's comment shows).If someone plants a flower, herb, shrub, berry, fruit, or tree that is supposed to to be hardy in zone 6b and it gets colder the following winter they just lost their plant(s). Not a huge loss since it was just a single growing season. But if it happens 5 years down the road then that is 5 years of growth for a woody plant that has just been lost. If that was a fruiting plant it may have just started fruiting or was about to. If it was a shade tree that could be 5 feet of growth or more, depending on species.Rodney", "images": []}}

title: Pre-finished or unfinished cabinets? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "donm-1967", "author_name": "Don M", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/donm-1967", "date": "2023-11-17", "text": "Hi all, Planning a kitchen remodel.  On past remodel jobs I've always purchased cabinets with a factory finish.  I see on many home improvement shows that they install unfinished cabinets and then painters spray them.  My first impression is that going the unfinished route is more cost effective, but factory finish would be better/more durable. Thoughts? Don", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "k8cd", "author_name": "k8cd", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/k8cd", "date": "2023-11-17", "text": "Great question!  Following in case someone answers.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "bry911", "author_name": "bry911", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bry911", "date": "2023-11-17", "text": "You will get many people who have never painted anything with strong opinions on this.  I suspect I have sprayed more paint than most people here and here is my 2 cents. Cost: Factory finishes are usually cheaper in apples to apples comparisons.  It takes a lot of extra labor to take all the painting equipment to the site, set up a decent environment, do al the prep work when the cabinets are already in place, etc. Durability: There is no advantage to either.  A 2k poly sprayed in a home will be exactly as durable as a 2k poly sprayed in a shop.  Same with all other coatings. Quality: There is certainly more quality control at a factory.  While it is not hard to get a factory quality coating in a home, there is not that much demand for it and so the market is flooded with house painters spraying inferior products on cabinets.  So you may struggle to find a decent cabinet painter. Safety: Many of the most durable products are not things you want hanging around the air in your home.  Conversion varnish is sometimes called canned respiratory distress and the Xylene used to catalyze it is a carcinogen.  Most 2k poly\u2019s use isocyanates which are safe after 24 - 48 hours but are hazardous before that. Finished product: The one advantage that site sprayed cabinets have is that the coating happens after the trim, filler, crown, etc.  The spraying also happens after shipping which means a bit more stable humidity.  You generally get a better looking finished product when done correctly.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "webuser-227031627", "author_name": "HU-227031627", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-227031627", "date": "2023-11-21", "text": "With pre-finished, you have a much better idea of what you are getting in advance.", "images": []}}

title: Need another side?  Gluten free Buffalo style cauliflower | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "plllog", "author_name": "plllog", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/plllog", "date": "2023-11-17", "text": "I've made this recipe a couple of times before and did it today because I needed to get the cauliflower out of my fridge, but I'm bored with cauliflower. https://feelgoodfoodie.net/recipe/buffalo-cauliflower-bites/ The difference today is that I subbed Anthony's Organic Buckwheat Flour (white).  Also, I didn't have any of the right kind of hot sauce, so I used Pace Medium, inc. the pieces of onion and peppers mixed with a goodly dash of TJ's habanero hot sauce  Probably between 1/2 and 1 tsp..  Nice heat, not scorching, but a different texture than usual.  I also didn't bother to level off the spices.  I mixed it up when I put the cauliflower in the oven, so by the time it was ready to have the sauce brushed on it was thick on the way to solidifying, which work great with a single layer of thick silicone bristles brush.  Getting the sauce on and sticking is always the hardest part, and other than a few wandering bits of onion and peppers it worked really well, and the flavor was outstanding. Finally, I cooked them to the charring point.  When I've made this before, it was too goopy. but tasty.  The buckwheat flour combined with a brave amount of oven time, made them crunchy and delectable.  And the cauliflower still had some tooth and wasn't reduced to mush. This is a total keeper, vegan and gluten free so easy to share,, and should rewarm well, but I'll have to let you know later on that. No picture because of the iPad issue and I'm too tired for the whole mailing rigamarole.", "images": []}

Yes, I suppose that I can replace things I do not like, but it is not really something I consider doing as long as whatever it is still works. Or works well enough anyway. title: PSA if you're on FB | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "gw-oakley", "author_name": "Oakley", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gw-oakley", "date": "2023-11-18", "text": "This was a first for me.  Years ago when it happened to DH he fell for it hook line and sinker, and he sunk.  :)   This happened on our individual PCs years apart. A few days ago I was reading FB, and the top right side has the Message icon and shows if I have any new messages.  Then I noticed about an inch away there was another Message icon, same as FB's, with 1 new message.  I thought it was a new feature of some sort so I clicked it. All of a sudden I got THE black screen which means new computer.  But the a blue Windows screen came on with the sound of sirens blasting and a robotic lady started telling me that my computer now has a Trojan.  At the top of the page it's in writing.  I almost had a heart attack when it happened. The instructions said do not turn your computer off and call the Microsoft Support number which was listed in large print.  My heart was still trying to escape my body.  There wasn't anywhere on the page where I could click it off.  I thought about ctrl alt delete but I didn't want to risk anything so I called the number. It was from Homestead, Florida and a man with an accent picked up the phone, there was a pause, then he said hello.  I was immediately suspicous because that's not how MS answers their phones.  I had to tell him about 5 times what was happening, I even turned the volume back up and put the phone to it so he could hear the lady talking.  I knew something was off but that's how a trojan can work.  He asked what type of device I'm using, and when he told me he can help me restore everything I was happy. He told me to find the search box at the bottom of the page which I didn't notice before, and told me to click on it.  I did and the only options it gave me was apps, websites, personal things like that.  I told him I had no clue what to choose and he told me he'll tell me what to type in the box. I asked what would happen if I did it and the dumb a$$ said it will link his computer to mine.  Idiot. main_question: {"author_id": "dedtired", "author_name": "dedtired", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dedtired", "date": "2023-11-18", "text": "Ive been wading my way through boxes and boxes of old family photos, trying to condense them. I have three photo portraits of unknown ancestors. They are in very old frames that are at least three inches thick and take up a lot of room. Id like to take the photos out of the frames to save space but I wonder if the frames are collectable. I feel kind of bad doing it but honestly there is no one who cares. Are the frames worth saving? I dont like tossing the frames but I dont know what else to do with them. Ideas?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/dea281770558cd2a_8541-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-761056975", "author_name": "Lola Bojackie", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-761056975", "date": "2023-11-21", "text": "May I expand on this topic, yet again? Putting aside photos of people you don't know for future generations to have... Why? If you don't know them, they certainly won't. And there's no way to find out who those people are. Anyone who might have had even an inkling of their names or their stories is most likely dead. Don't burden future generations with stuff. Stuff they don't need. Stuff they don't want. Stuff that will only cause generational guilt and will continue to be passed along to the next person. But for what? It's just taking up space for no reason. I highly recommend Marie Kondo's book on getting rid of clutter. I understand that photos have a way of tugging at our hearts - but seriously - there is no love from the photograph's subject for you - you were probably born after they died and they'd have no idea who you are. There is no \"love\" in those photos. They're just pieces of paper with images. Throwing them away or burning them - or even selling them to antique vendors or on eBay - is fine. There's truly no need to keep them, especially if you're only \"hoping\" a relative will want them. The same goes with ANYTHING that's left behind. I am an only child. My mother was an only child. Her mother's siblings had no children, so EVERYTHING that could be \"passed down\" went to my mom and then to me. At one time I had five sets of china and silver, and three sets of crystal. I had eight sets of everyday dinnerware. It was ridiculous. When my dad died (my mom had died years prior), we had a 6-hour estate sale and got rid of EVERYTHING. What didn't sell went straight to Goodwill. The burden of survivorship is hard enough without the expectation that someone's \"wishes\" or \"expectations\" will have to be honored. Yes, this is a soapbox topic for me.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "greggbrighton", "author_name": "Gregg Morris", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/greggbrighton", "date": "2023-11-18", "text": "We\u2019ve just had new timber sashes fitted in 4 different bays windows. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "chrismojo", "author_name": "Chris Morgan-Jones", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/chrismojo", "date": "2023-11-18", "text": "There are numerous options, all with different costs and benefits. Here are some thoughts based on things I\u2019ve done before. If your final finish is going to be wood panelling then stud work infilled with rockwool insulation or kingspan thermal insulation board (or similar) is probably the way to go. The insulation boards do have a foil backing and therefore resist water penetration fairly well. If there are damp issues then these should be resolved before insulating. Take the opportunity to sort out any pointing and then consider a treatment such as Bostik damp-proofer. If your final finish is going to be plaster then an insulated plasterboard is a good option. The great news is that it looks basically un-remuddled, so you can focus on repais and putting things to rights without having to undo a whole lot of misguided \"updating\".  Lots of original looking detail which is great, and makes your job much easier. As with any such project you start by mitigating any serious structural issues. Make sure your foundations and sills are sound, that water isn't entering the building anywhere, and that the roof, gutters, and drainage are good. Then move on to any areas with rot-- figure out why it happened and correct the cause before going after the rot itself. I'm guessing a northerly climate, so putting in some energy efficiency that wasn't there originally is probably a priority. If your local utility offers energy audits take advantage of them. In many places there is substantial financial assistace for upgrading air sealing and insulation. Once you've tightened the building up as much as you can and added as much insulation as makes sense you can address mechanical systems-- hopefully you'll end up needing much smaller heat sources than before. Once structure is stabilized it's time to think about how the space works for you and your family, and which aspects of the interior need work. Lot's of folks here can help with that. One useful maxim that's helped me through many restoration projects is \"don't destroy good old work\". That said, kitches and baths need to be made functional. The list goes on and on-- it's nice to dream about paint colors, but for most of us that's a choice way down the road. main_question: {"author_id": "gold-gold40", "author_name": "gold gold", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gold-gold40", "date": "2023-11-19", "text": "Understanding the Fortune 500 Fortune magazine was founded in 1929 by Henry Robinson Luce.1  The first issue was published the following year and has since become one of the world's leading business publications. Originally printed monthly, the magazine put out 16 issues every year and also has a major presence online. The magazine compiled its first list of the most successful American companies\u2014both public and private\u2014in 1955. It was created by editor Edgar P. Smith in an effort to measure the size and power of American businesses during a time when the country's economic power was \"the envy of the world.\"2  Originally called the Fortune Industrial 500, the name of the list was shortened to Fortune 500. The Fortune 500 survey includes companies that are incorporated and operate in the United States and file financial statements with government agencies. This includes companies that are both publicly traded and privately held. Private companies that don't file financial statements with government agencies, foreign corporations are excluded, as are American companies consolidated by other companies and those that neglect to report full financial statements for at least three quarters of the current fiscal year.3  As of 2020, companies are ranked by total revenues for their respective fiscal years as reported on their 10-K filings or comparable financial statements. https://stockstrategy.net/ Stock Strategy Stock trading Strategy About two-thirds of the Fortune 500 appear on the S&P 500 Index, so consider an S&P 500 index fund if you want to invest in many of these companies. More than 1,800 American companies have been featured on the list over the course of its history. The list has changed dramatically from the very first Fortune 500.4  Mergers and acquisitions (M&A), shifts in production output, and bankruptcies have taken companies off of the list. The impact of a recession can also take out multiple companies from individual sectors. The Fortune 500 list can often be a telling sign of how strong the economy is or if there has been an economic recovery after poor performing years. Special Considerations As of 2020, Walmart (WMT) took to the top spot on the Fortune 500 list for the eighth year in a row. The company earned revenue of $524 billion.5  Online retailer Amazon (AMZN) took the second spot with revenues of $280.5 billion, jumping up four spots from 2019.6  Exxon Mobil (XOM) came in third with revenues of $265 billion, while Apple (AAPL) and CVS Health (CVS) ranked in fourth and fifth.7 The three most profitable companies on the 2020 list were as follows: Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.A/BRK.B) with net profits of $81.4 billion Apple with net profits of $55.2 billion Microsoft (MSFT) with net profits of $39.2 billion Notable newcomers to the list include Dow (DOW), Baker Hughes (BKR), and Uber (UBER). The History of the Fortune 500 As noted above, the idea for the list came from Edgar P. Smith, who was an assistant managing editor for Fortune. Smith's idea took off and provided the grounds for the popular annual list.2  The original Fortune 500 lists contained only companies that were in the manufacturing, mining, and energy sectors, limiting inclusion for many big-name companies. To secure a spot on the list, a company had to produce $49.7 million in annual revenue.4  In the original 1955 Fortune 500 list, General Motors (GM) was the top company with annual revenues of $9.8 billion. https://stockstrategy.net/ Stock Strategy Stock trading Strategy The Fortune 500 underwent its biggest change in 1995. title: Load bearing or decorative | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-371560545", "author_name": "HU-371560545", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-371560545", "date": "2023-11-19", "text": "Want to remove the half wall/shelves with columns to open up our space. I assume they're not load bearing as they run parallel with the joists and I can't imagine the columns are supporting much by sitting on such a thin edge of the shelf. Thoughts?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "palimpsest", "author_name": "palimpsest", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/palimpsest", "date": "2023-11-20", "text": "What do you hope to achieve by removing it? It will make the doorway between the two rooms bigger but it will still be a doorway. Right now it probably gives you a little more wall space to put furniture next to on the sitting room side. Sometimes removal of any wall space makes furniture placement more difficult or at least doesn't improve furniture placement. Many people here remove the tiny vestibules at their front door to open things up, and now you walk right into the living room and nobody really wants to put a chair or anything backing up to the front door. When there was a wall there, they could have furniture 6-8\" away from the front door, because there was a wall in between. It opens things up, but not in a way that helps. These are just things to think about. Sometimes in a small house it takes away space by trying to turn it into a big open area. If you *do remove it, take it apart very carefully and store it in the attic or basement.", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mamiller040256", "author_name": "M Miller", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mamiller040256", "date": "2023-11-19", "text": "@Ann Crisp - the regulars on this forum know that is @Lomo's M.O. - to criticize the homeowner for not spending $100k on a kitchen, and to project assumptions onto them.  In any case, for the problems at hand, just to be clear, typically a handyman is not a licensed electrician.  If they were, they'd be an electrician full time, not a handyman.  It depends on your state, but in general, a licensed electrician must have completed an approved 2-year program in the electrical trade, and then apprentice with a master electrician for 4 years.  From what you have said, it looks like your General Contractor did not bother to use a licensed electrician the way he should have as part of the project.  It is up to you to hire one. When my receptacles were installed in the backsplash, the house's masonry was just behind the backer board, and so the receptacle boxes would not fit. I am not at all saying that is your issue with that one receptacle - it's just that you need more than a handyman to address it. Regarding the tile work, I always advise on this forum - as this issue comes up many times - never to use the GC's tiler.  Always delete the backsplash tile from the project's Scope of Work, and separately hire a tiler yourself.  The reason for this is that when you hire a tiler yourself, you know that is what they do 100% of their time. Your Cloe tile is characterized by its irregular, more handmade-looking appearance.  That makes it harder to install than a consistent exactly rectangular tile.  It needs a better installer.  You can get the GC to come back and make corrections.  But you can't be sure that their expertise is just not up to it.  Hard to know.  If you find that is the problem, you will have to hire a tiler yourself to make corrections. A \"change of plane\" means the joint where the vertical backsplash meets the horizontal counter.  It's not only a change in plane, but a change in materials and those material move at different rates.  That joint will always have movement. title: Transporting House Plants Cross-Country In A Cold Car | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "aaron-watson22", "author_name": "A W", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/aaron-watson22", "date": "2023-11-19", "text": "Hello, I have kind of a sad problem. I have a few larger tropical and desert plants that have some sentimental value. I am moving cross-country on Thursday, from upstate New York to Arizona, and I would like to take them with me. Unfortunately, the forecast lows locally will be around 30F, with highs of 45, making transportation risky, but I don't really think I have a lot of other options ATM. Flying with them is not practical, and shipping is cost-prohibitive given the size. I am sending my car on a car carrier, and am considering loading them into the back, which would mean I need to solve for cold shock. Transit time would be four days. They are currently potted. I am considering a solution where I would fit them into a 70-gallon tote with some number of 72-hour heatpacks to make a sort of mini-greenhouse, but I am honestly not sure if this would either solve the temperature issue *or* introduce a new deadly issue with lack of fresh air. Has anyone been in this position and succeeded? How did you do it?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "aaron-watson22", "author_name": "A W", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/aaron-watson22", "date": "2023-12-12", "text": "Petrushka, since you suggested a follow-up: What I ended up doing was packing the smaller plants in 12x12x18 boxes, and the larger yucca in a pair of 20x20x20 boxes. I chose these dimensions based on what I measured I could fit in the car, as three 12\" boxes would fit side by side in the back of my car's cargo area, and the 40\" box sideways in the back seat. The draecana was actually three separate young draecana stems, so I chose the healthiest and straightest one that looked like it would fit in the box potted, and gave the other two away. The pots were secured in place with crumbled packing paper, and since the yucca was going on the side, I also packed the lip of the pot with packing paper then taped a \"lid\" of paper over it to secure the soil tightly. This was very effective, and the box did end up fitting perfectly in the car, with the aid of a Rubbermaid bin to get it tipped up into place. Two hours before the car carrier arrived, in the large box, I placed three 72-hour heat packs, and in each of the small boxes, I placed one. I taped them shut loosely, then placed heavy blankets (a down comforter on the smaller plants, a quilt and some sheets on the yucca) loosely over them with two more heat packs underneath each. The rationale here was that if the boxes outran their oxygen supply and quit reacting (a known issue with heat packs), the outer heat packs might at least keep producing an insulating warm layer under the blankets. I was anxious about this since, when the day came, a 96-hour trip was projected due to weather, with the last night scheduled to be a winter storm. I was hoping for the best as it was too late to change plans.. Fortunately, the car carrier arrived in Arizona a day early, but still had to cross the Rocky Mountains in an overnight snowstorm with the lowest temperatures of the journey. When the car arrived, all heat packs were cold and hard. (Some heated back up after some time with the boxes open, which indicates to me that they did run out of oxygen and stopped reacting before they ran out of chemicals.) The boxes were cold and clammy to the touch, and the pots felt chilled. However, as far as I can tell, no casualties. The croton, the plant I assumed I was likely to lose, has somehow not defoliated at all. In fact, it apparently loves Arizona and began producing new foliage from all but the tallest stem within a few days. The one \"victim\" was the draecana, which I had had to repot at the last minute to remove its neighbors and situate it low enough in the pot to fit in the box. This was poor planning on my part. I believe the stress of this, combined with the cold shock, was pretty severe, and it has lost around 20 leaves. However, the top half, while a little off-color and ill-looking, is still full and seems like it's trying to hang in there and make a comeback. Since it is now alone and I needed to repot it to a normal depth in fresh mix anyway, I down-sized it into the croton's old 10\" pot, and gave the croton some more space to thrive in the draecana's pot. The draecana is sitting on my desk for a while where it can get some nice bright window light. TL;DR: This can definitely be done, if you absolutely must and the timing is aligned in your favor. Check the weather, measure boxes carefully, pack securely, and make sure you have plenty of heatpacks of the correct duration.", "images": []}}

title: Remodeling a home lacking HVAC ducting | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jdpyn2", "author_name": "John 9a", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jdpyn2", "date": "2023-11-21", "text": "The home I'm remodeling for my retirement began as a double wide mobile home.  My dad had an addition added to the mobile home about 30 years ago.  I will be wrecking the mobile home and putting a garage in its footprint.  The addition is structurally sound but needed roofing, windows, new sheetrock, flooring, and some electrical changes.  There is no HVAC unit or duct work and the ceilings are wood and I'm hoping to preserve that one feature and not build boxing or the like to house ducting.  The home is smallish, around 1,500 sq. ft. and is basically a two-story cube.  My concept is to build in a few (maybe four) inter-wall low-velocity fans to create a circulation of air from a vaulted ceiling main room on the north side of the house and around the south rooms and back to the vaulted ceilinged main room.  The vaulted ceilinged room will probably have a wood stove so the vaulted area of that ceiling will be warmer and available to circulate to other parts of the house.  I see options to either create two circular paths of air flow, one for each floor, or another option of a single, more tortuous path of flow that might include two floor/ceiling passages.  I have found fans built for interwall air exchange and believe I could create a single electrical circuit to control the fans with a single switch or timer.  I will probably install a mini-split AC unit, also in the vaulted main room. Sorry for the long post but hopefully that covers my concept. Eventually its roots grew through the pot into the ground and the pot was leaning. The tree spent at least 14 years of its life in a pot. Five years ago someone offered to plant the tree in the ground for us and we agreed without researching the tree. He cut the roots that had grown out of the pot and replanted it directly in the ground. The tree very quickly went into shock and lost all its leaves, but fully recovered within a few months. The tree is doing very well now. Tree is near San Diego, so no cold winters or anything like that to harm it. I have noticed one root showing in the lawn surface for about 12 inches, but otherwise no roots are visible. The tree is about 25 feet from the house, but only 4 feet from a cinder block wall. The sewer lines don't run through the backyard, so my main concerns are that the tree could damage the wall, irrigation pipes, get into the neighbor's yard, or possibly get under the house. When we first moved in, it was enough to startle us awake at night. As soon as it rains, the sound continues for hours. What could be a solution to this? I'm currently considering borrowing a ladder and placing a sponge wrapped with a thick towel on that pipe and pressing it down with a heavy brick, but is there a better way? https://youtube.com/shorts/nZCTUqLnsjM?si=GDMpxpNC53y2yN4Y", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/8f125a66055e4d7c_9041-w500-h682-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2a721d9c055e4000_5588-w500-h888-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

I wouldn't do that.  No, I wouldn't want all the rainshed from the 2nd story gutter getting dumped on that bit of roof.  Not with windows, a vertical wall and a sidewall in such close proximity to the downspout. Perhaps replacing that small run of metal downspout across the roof with PVC downspout might reduce the drip noise to a tolerable level but I don't know if PVC will match up with the metal fittings sizewise. Lots of things you could use to insulate the existing but the trick is to not create an eyesore.  Automotive sound deadening material wired in place.  Carpet pad scraps wired in place.   Bubble wrap.  Or foil faced bubble wrap insulation.  All ugly. Best that I can come up with is to make a U-Shaped cover out of foam board insulation.  Glue together with caulk or polyurethane glue.  Size it for a friction fit and add a bit of caulk, adhesive in a couple of spots.  Paint it to approximate the roof color...any acrylic paint, even craft paint.  The paint will help to protect the foam board from UV degradation.  But that won't be 100%...there will still be some noise. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-61174020661", "author_name": "A A", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-61174020661", "date": "2023-11-24", "text": "HelloI got this ponytail palm 7 months ago from Ikea. It was never repotted. I have it sitting by a north facing window and water it every 2 to 4 weeks. Last time I watered was a week ago with a few drops of organic fertilizer from The Grow Co. And I really let it sit in the water. I realized about 1.5 months ago that it doesn't seem to have much soil in the pot. The leaves have been steadily losing color. So I thought maybe it's dehydrated. But even after a good soak, they're still looking more diseased. There was dirt all over the leaves, so I showered just the leaves today. Or maybe leave it?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ecf192460560df3a_7422-w500-h888-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/fd71c3590560df3d_7424-w500-h888-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c761cfd60560df40_7428-w500-h888-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c681fe670560df42_7429-w500-h888-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/ae9105720560df45_7435-w500-h888-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2023-11-24", "text": "If what you show in photo #3 is what came out of the current pot intact, then yes, it is severely pot bound. And contrary to what you may have read, no plant prefers to be pot bound. You would not find that happening under natural growing conditions so why should it be any different as a potted houseplant? It needs a slightly larger pot with a fast draining soil mix, something you would use for cacti and succulents. I grow almost exclusively in containers, indoors and out, and I rarely pay a lot of attention to the time of year when repotting, except for very temperate climate plants that go through a full dormancy - Beaucarnea do not. The root congestion and lack of any visible potting soil would indicate that a) the plant may be drying out too quickly/a need to bump up the watering frequency. Drought tolerant or not, plants need to be able to access moisture as their biology demands and there is nothing visible to support any degree of soil moisture under current growing conditions. And b) there is nothing to provide any nutrient supplementation. Plants grown in containers with a soil-less mix will require you to provide nutrients on a pretty regular schedule regardless of time of year. I seriously doubt it is any sort of disease and I see no signs of spider mites (stippling and webbing). It just needs repotting. Fortunately, @opaone has covered part of what I might cover.  I'll try to be a tad succinct by incorporating by reference the many hood and MUA topics addressed on this forum. On leakage.  While opaone is the IAQ expert here, and not me, my choice is to not keep the house inordinately tight, as various stuff one might own or build with can out-gas less than helpful fumes.  Also in spite of the most heroic kitchen ventilation, some cooking effluent can escape, at least into the local kitchen air. And a gas range or cooktop will have a much higher level of non-food effluent that has to be captured and contained than, say, an induction cooktop.  We can't, as far as I know, compare the monetary value of life shortening due to combustion product inhalation to the monetary cost of heating replacement air due to leakiness of the house or over-performing MUA used to try to minimize the gas products. On the hood. To aid capture of the rising and expanding cooking plumes, it is desirable to have the hood extend beyond the edges of the cooking zone.  For wall mounts, this means both sides and front (cook's side).  Hence, a 48-inch cooktop with pans that might extend to the edges, one needs roughly 3 inches of side extension on each side.  Front to back depends on counter depth and cooking layout, but I would go for at least 24 inches.  So we need a hood entry area of 4.5 x 2 = 9 sq. ft. To ensure containment of the captured plumes, I recommend for residential hoods and residential cooking that includes hot oil or grease cooking such as searing or stir frying, that the hood entry aperture have a 90 ft/min flow velocity across the entry.  This implies a 9 x 90 = 810 CFM air volumetric flow rate. Because blowers, whether internal, in-line, wall, or roof have flow rates that vary with the pressure across the blower, and because blowers are rated in free air (zero static pressure), the rated blower flow rate has to be higher.  How much higher can be determined by analysis if all the losses vs. flow rate are known, or can be crudely estimated by using a factor of 1.5.  This implies the blower rating should be 1200 CFM, not 900.  It also assumes that the house is not sealed up, but has an MUA system keeping the internal pressure within some small difference of the outside pressure.  Pressure drop (loss) seen by the hood blower is that of the loop from cooktop to outside to inside to cooktop.  See explanatory graph; click to expand. I wouldn't recommend a powered damper on the hood path although I don't know that it is prohibited. On the hood duct. Hood ducts carry grease laden air and a balance is needed between grease impingement collection on the duct walls and condensation collection on the duct walls.  Duct air velocity (CFM/sectional area) should be within the range of 1000 to 2000 ft/min.  [ @aklogcabin was 2-inches a typo?] On make-up air. The two main purposes of make-up air are (a) safety -- avoiding back-drafting combustion appliances, and (b) allowing the hood blower to operate near the flow rate that the hood system pressure losses alone would limit.  An actual 800 CFM hood blower will need an actual 800 CFM MUA blower, or a big hole in the wall.  The acceptability of the latter will depend on combustion appliances.  If they have their own MUA or are otherwise isolated from the kitchen somewhat more house pressure differential may be tolerated. At a minimum, the MUA system needs a heater, filter, and damper.  For MUA a motorized damper is common.  If pressure loss has to be made up, then a blower providing, at the MUA path pressure loss, 800 CFM. MUA heating is only needed during operation, and during much of the cooking at less than full power.  See the graph for the requirement. MUA has to be introduced into the house so that turbulence at the cooktop is minimized.  One extreme that works is to introduce it away from the kitchen via a long hallway or other path. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "buehl", "author_name": "Buehl", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/buehl", "date": "2023-11-26", "text": "Yes, the layout is inefficient.  I don't know what you have now, but even if you have a similar layout now, think about how you can make it better. I know some people say to do what you want or plan around how you cook/prep now.  However, that doesn't mean it's the best functional layout -- it's just what you're used to and have adapted to.  It may be, but maybe not.  It helps to understand our adaptability and our resistance to change -- both of which apply to everyone to some extent. Human beings are very adaptable. We can adapt to anything - good or bad!  We adapt so well that we tell ourselves it's fine the way it is and we often no longer \"see\" the issues we've adapted to.  But, what if it could be better?  If you ask just about anyone here who took our advice and changed their layout to make it better, they will tell you they never realized it could be so much better and wondered how they had lived with the issues for so long!  (The answer is back to the adaptability of human beings!) Human beings are resistant to change. Even when something can be made better, we resist change.  We like what we know and we have a hard time seeing other ways to do things - even if they would be so much better!  And, as I mentioned before, we've adapted to what we have - both the good and the bad. Why not at least try for something better? Think about what you are saying are must-haves -- are they really the best layout for the space? It may also help to understand workflow and how much time we spend in each work zone. Workflow: Refrigerator > Sink > Prep Counterspace (preferably directly adjacent to the sink) > Range/Cooktop/Oven Work done/time spent in each primary work zone: Based on the above, the zone that should be in the most desirable location is the Prep Zone where the majority of your work is done.  (Cleaning up doesn't really include much sink work anymore, so it's location isn't as important as it used to be pre-DW days.)", "images": []}}

title: Historic bungalow kitchen renovation - feedback, please? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "eah03", "author_name": "eah03", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/eah03", "date": "2023-11-25", "text": "Hi, all- In beginning stages of planning kitchen renovation for my 100 yr old casita/Spanish bungalow & would be grateful for any feedback or advice on my initial (& very pedestrian!) design sketch.  The home is in a historic district that prevents me from ever expanding the footprint or making exterior changes. The main level is a compact 900 sq ft, with 2 bedrooms & 1 bath on west half of house & small kitchen, living & dining rooms stacked on east side of house. I have decided to combine the kitchen & dining areas to create a larger kitchen space, for a total footprint of ~19\u2019 x ~14\u2019. A few notes/priorities driving my design planning: -I want to maintain the historic/vintage feel of the house as much as possible. Kitchen cabinets will be full height inset Shaker style (mirroring the style of existing/original built in cabinets). -Storage is a priority. I am tall (nearly 6\u2019) and higher/taller cabinets aren\u2019t a problem for me to navigate. -I own quite a bit of baking/cooking tools & equipment, & want to be able to store as much stuff as possible behind cabinets. Clear counter space is important to me, especially in such a small space. This is a concern as related to appliance selection to some degree as well. I don\u2019t think I have space for a wall oven; as a frequent baker, will I regret this? I also have never used a microwave drawer, & my design incorporates one at the business end of the island. As a tall person, I think I\u2019d prefer my microwave higher/closer to eye level, but don\u2019t know where else it could easily live without compromising counter & storage space. -I love to cook, and especially love to bake. I will invest in pro style appliances & high end finishes. I expect this will be my \u201cforever\u201d kitchen, and am more focused on designing for my lifestyle & preferences than for resale value. -I live alone, so my kitchen is rarely bustling with people. I do frequently entertain small groups very informally (football game watching, etc) & we always gravitate to the kitchen.  Because of the small size of my home, I want my kitchen to serve as a multipurpose room. -the east side of the house faces a lovely park & the room gets great light. There is an exterior side door at the NE corner of the kitchen that faces this park & gets more use than my primary front door. This existing exterior door will be replaced with an OUTswing Dutch door. -Denver has great weather, and I enjoy cooking with the door/windows open - including the large original casement window facing the park. Unfortunately, this window is an INswing window, which can be intrusive in a small room when opened. I have always liked the idea of having a window seat with storage under this window, & want to be able to continue to open the window (if not fully, at least partially). -I frequently use the fireplace in the small sitting/front entry room directly south of the kitchen space. I do not want to combine the kitchen, dining AND sitting room to create a full open concept space, so I preserved a wall between the new kitchen and entry room with 2 passages through to the kitchen. It\u2019s a quirky design, but I like being able to enjoy glimpses of the fire when in the kitchen & also plan to use the sitting room area in front of the fire as a formal dining area  occasionally for larger groups. The double passage will allow for easier traffic flow & serving between these rooms on those occasions, & also gives me sufficient wall space on the south kitchen wall between the doorways for a large TV. *I recognize several of my design elements run afoul of modern kitchen design spacing recommendations (ex- suggested width of kitchen \u201ctraffic lanes\u201d). For the most part, I am ok with this. I\u2019ve lived in several small, historic homes over the last 30 years and know it\u2019s simply not always realistic to apply modern standards to these small spaces. I am now accustomed to old house quirks and compromises and, for example, am willing to sacrifice some lane clearance around the island. I\u2019ve used pre-Houzz Garden Web as a research resource for years , but am not a frequent or savvy poster; apologies in advance for \u201cnot knowing what I don\u2019t know\u201d! My vision for this remodel is pretty clear in terms of what I like & don\u2019t want, but know there are tips & details I\u2019ve not considered thought that would help advance some of my above goals. Thanks in advance!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/272225410562724f_0611-w500-h620-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

main_question: {"author_id": "kara-dial", "author_name": "Kara M", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kara-dial", "date": "2023-11-26", "text": "We had an central a/c leak into the floor in July. 3 yard diameter right in the middle of the house. insurance approved all flooring to be replaced except the back two bedrooms. We found a reputable contractor through two family friends who said he would work with insurance to replace any subfloor and get any additional items needed approved throughout the job. The flooring crew, directed by the second in charge to the contractor, replaced the damaged particle board with plywood. This turned out to be unlevel, leaving low spots and ridges. They used adhesive in at least one spot of vinyl plank which seeped through the planks and left spots. A plank in a closet even cracked. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-442933329", "author_name": "Steve Harris", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-442933329", "date": "2023-11-26", "text": "I have a Fisher & Paykel Ecosmart washing machine (model GWL10US) from around 2001 that worked reliably until 2011 when it had issues starting the cycle. I had it fixed and the service order shows a fault code of 131 and a replacement of the rotor position sensor (part 420296P). From the service manual: \"131. (10000011) Repetitive Rotor Position Sensor Error\" After that fix it worked great for the last 12 years, but just started having issues starting again. It's intermittent in that if I keep trying I can get it to eventually start and when it starts it gets through the entire cycle without issue. When I see the startup failing it displays the same code as before (10000011). Surprisingly, if I enter diagnostic mode right after this error there are no fault codes shown. I reached out to the same repair person I had used before expecting that he'd just want to replace the rotor position sensor again, but after explaining everything this was his response: \"According to tech support the original fault code will remain until a new fault will replace it (even if you unplug it). So I'm thinking you don't need the sensor. And usually fault code 131 is not intermittent like yours is behaving. The three things it could be are the controller, wiring issue or the pump drawing too much amps & causing a power surge. In 25 years of doing Fisher Paykel I think I've only changed 3-4 wiring harnesses. My hunch it's that, because of the intermittent issue. But it could be the controller itself & or the pump. Unfortunately it's a trial and error at this point\" Does that analysis sound correct? That makes it sound like I could be spending a lot in repairs that might not even help, so perhaps at this point I should just get a new washer? I like the idea of keeping it running given how reliable it's been over the past 20 years, but the idea of spending $500 or more and still having a broken washing machine doesn't sound like a good idea.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "dadoes", "author_name": "dadoes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dadoes", "date": "2023-11-27", "text": "The basket rotates during fill so an RPS problem would manifest then. Try other cycles to confirm the problem is consistent, although behavior is the same on all of them during fill.  Permanent Press doesn't run the initial Eco Active treatment, fills straight-away for an agitated wash. You can bypass the lid switch to see what's happening inside by placing a strong-enough magnet at the edge of machine top aligned with the protrusion where the trigger magnet is located on the edge of the lid.  A refrigerator magnet may not be quite sufficient strength. What happens if you select Regular (or any cycle) and advance directly to the final spin before starting?  There's no filling in that case, the pump will turn on and the motor pulse CC/CCW to confirm via inertia that the basket is engaged for spin, then spin will proceed. The pump squeal indicates bad bearings on it.  Spraying it with WD-40 is a temporary bandage.  It needs to be replaced, especially if there's any leaking which entails a large risk of damaging the windings or electrically shorting it which also entails a risk of damaging the motor board (that's not supposed to happen but can).  If no leaking, you could try applying some oil to the pump bearings but that typically also isn't a long-term fix.  Keep in mind that WD-40 is a solvent moreso than a lubricant.  It leaves a bit of light lubricant when the carrier dries but that's not adequate to oil motor bearings. There's no way to directly test the RPS without a special electronic service tool. I'm not sure it'll work on GWL10 as there's no reference in the service manual until the next series GWL11 ... multiple levels of diagnostic info via the cycle progress lights per which spin LEDs are lit.  One of the levels reports motor RPM/10 per the binary coding.  You could try it if you wish to see if anything is indicated.  Get in Diagnostics, adjust Spin Up/Down for Fast, Slow, and Hold lit.  Rotate the basket and note if the cycle progress lights flash accordingly. An RPS problem could be the RPS is bad, a wire is broken, or the contacts on the RPS or its harness connector are dirty/corroded.  Access to the RPS requires removing the motor rotor, and then removing the stator from bottom of the tub.  The RPS can be damaged by an electrostatic zap so handle accordingly.", "images": []}}

Anyway, I rooted a cutting of it a few years ago, and it is now growing on the back fence of our new garden. I thought it was about 8-10ft high, but last week our gardeners found a couple of canes of it had grown to the top of the old privet tree (20-25 ft off the ground) next to the fence (they were pruning the privet tree to let more light into the garden). It was hard to find a place for such a large rose in our 1/3rd acre lot, and I was afraid that it would not get enough light to get really big, but it is on its way! They have been in use for centuries, long before any plastic was ever available, and with generally excellent results. Plastic pots tend to become water saturated,  especially when soil media or watering practices are not ideal.  Terra cotta drains freely, both from any drainage holes as well via the clay itself. Because of this porosity, which plastic lacks, terra cotta or clay pots are able to \"breathe\", allowing easy oxygen exchange and cooling potting soils in hot summer climates. I also have few concerns about your choice of potting media. Commercial, prepared potting soils are for the most part unsuitable, which is one of the primary reasons experienced container gardeners tend to make their own. Provided yours contains enough perlite and coarse sand, it should be very free draining yet adequately moisture retentive and that should suit the salvia well. It is not full evergreen, even in its native environment, and it will freely drop leaves well into  the late part of the season in response to shorter days and cooling temps. It could also be a watering issue........best not to rely on any sort of schedule but water thoroughly only as needed. The need to water can be determined by a 'tell' or simply by testing the weight of the pot - if heavy, skip; if lightweight, then give a good drink. title: Rugosa Roses, Anyone? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "karen-service", "author_name": "Karen Service", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/karen-service", "date": "2023-11-27", "text": "Many years ago I went to visit a cousin in Ohio who had a magnificent herb garden. In it she had a couple massive rugosa roses that she grew for their fragrant petals and their hips. I was duly impressed! I thought of getting one while we still lived in Utah but we left before I got the chance and believed they wouldn't grow here in eastern Tn. Fast forward to now- I had a chance to get a bare-root own-root rugosa this spring and decided to try one called Schneekoppe (Snow Pavement, I think). I planted it in a pot and moved it to a spot that was sunny from about 10 till about 3. This summer we had everything you could imagine weather-wise: drought, then buckets of rain with some memorable storms, then drought again. So far, so good. It has looked good throughout the summer and then through the fall. At one point in late spring it even had buds but thanks to some voracious deer, I didn't get to see them open. So question #1: I plan on planting it in the center of a raised shrub bed which it will share with a couple sweet boxes, a tree peony, a sasanqua camellia, a native rhododendron minus and I think, an interspecies peony. My hope is that it will grow wider than tall and fill in the center of this bed. It will get maybe an hour less full sun than it gets currently and dappled shade for the rest of the day. Will it be OK with that? Will it stay under 6'? It seems like a YMMV kind of a rose and it's hard to get a straight answer. Question #2- It's a far cry from potting soil to our soil. Although I'm constantly working to improve it, it is thin, rocky and very acidic. On the plus side, our drainage is great. I plan on adding compost, one of the 'Tones'  and some mulch from time to time but for truly heavy feeders, they'll never be happy here. Is this a rose that can cope? Question #3- Is this rose a once-bloomer? I'm fine with it either way. Will its leaves color up in the fall? Thanks for any experience you can share.", "images": []}

That's possibly because it was dead headed just about 'til September. What impressed me the most about my Schneekoppe was its cupped, well shaped blooms, unlike so many Rugosas which have unkept, blousy petals in their blooms. The repeat was quick and the bush nicely shaped.  As most Rugosa bushes do, they send out runners making a colony rather than basal growth from the crown.  The runners can come up about a foot from the original bush.  They are not rampant, but part of the Rugosa growth habit that needs to be considered. title: Créer une 4eme chambre | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-47293479", "author_name": "Pauline D.", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-47293479", "date": "2023-11-27", "text": "Bonjour \u00e0 tous, Mon appartement dispose actuellement de 3 chambres. La chambre 1 est une suite parentale avec une sdb attenante. La chambre 3 est le bureau de mon mari qui travaille \u00e0 la maison. La chambre 2 est pour le moment celle de mes 3 filles. Ma fille ain\u00e9e, devenue adolescente, souhaiterait avoir sa propre chambre. J'ai envisag\u00e9 plusieurs solutions pour cr\u00e9er une 4\u00e8me chambre, car mon mari a besoin de conserver une pi\u00e8ce ferm\u00e9e pour pouvoir travailler au calme. 1 - couper la grande chambre en 2 pour faire 2 chambres, ou une chambre et un bureau, mais je n'aime pas trop les pi\u00e8ces en enfilade et en second jour. 2 - Cr\u00e9er une cuisine ouverte dans le salon et transformer la cuisine actuelle en chambre, mais je trouve que cela r\u00e9duit beaucoup la pi\u00e8ce \u00e0 vivre, et je pr\u00e9f\u00e8re avoir une cuisine ferm\u00e9e ou semi-ouverte. 3 - Couper la chambre des mes filles en deux en gardant une partie chambre c\u00f4t\u00e9 fen\u00eatre et en d\u00e9pla\u00e7ant la cuisine dans l'autre partie. L'acc\u00e8s \u00e0 la chambre se fait soit par le salon, soit par la cuisine, ce dont je ne suis pas trop fan. En plus, je ne peux pas ouvrir compl\u00e8tement la partie cuisine sur le s\u00e9jour car le mur entre le salon et la chambre 2 est porteur. La cuisine sera donc soit en second jour ou soit semi ouverte sur le couloir. Cela ne me satisfait pas pleinement. Auriez-vous d'autres id\u00e9es qui ne n\u00e9cessitent pas trop de travaux ? J'esp\u00e8re que le plan sera lisible. Je pr\u00e9cise que la fen\u00eatre au centre du mur de 7m dans le salon est une porte fen\u00eatre, ainsi que celle dans la chambre 2.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/de32cd4e05648dc3_8730-w500-h281-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Help! Gutter hangers installed over shingles on a new roof | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-398490807", "author_name": "A G", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-398490807", "date": "2023-11-28", "text": "I hired a general contractor to do a whole house renovation on a 1910 wood farmhouse, including a new roof using CertainTeed architectural asphalt shingles.  They called after they had removed most of the roof and said the crown was rotted through and needed to be replaced.   They said they needed to finish the roof that day because of heavy rain in the forecast.  Because the crown would have to be fabricated and installed, they said they would need to install the gutter hangers over the shingles, instead of under them.  At first I agreed, but then I read online that this is a major defect and will cause leaks.  I pushed back and they said no problem, after the crown is installed, we can lift the shingles and install the gutter with the hangers underneath the shingles, as you're supposed to do.  Fabricating and installing the crown took a couple of months.  When they finally were ready to install the gutters, they put the hangers on top of the shingles, nailing or screwing through the asphalt, ice and water shield, and plywood.  They didn't use any sealant or silicone on the nails.  It looks terrible.  They claimed that the shingles were melted to the roof from the heat and couldn't be lifted without tearing.  They want to install a layer of shingle over the hangers using some kind of sealant.  This might look marginally better but wouldn't this cause ice dams and more likely result in leaks? I think this is clearly a defect that needs to be addressed, but I don't know the best way to repair the problem. I like the contractor a lot and most of their work has been very good.  They are highly respected in the area and also very expensive.  There's more work to be done on the project and I need to maintain the relationship. But I'm worried they have created a major problem that I would like them to fix. Any advice would be greatly appreciated!!", "images": []}

title: Where to put the dryer vent hookup behind stackables in a tight nook? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jillius18", "author_name": "Jillius", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jillius18", "date": "2023-11-28", "text": "Hi everyone.  We are at the tail end of shifting the hookups for our washer dryer to this nook (pictured below) where we're going to have a stackable washer/dryer.   Since this is a small nook, and I have PTSD from installing stackables into an unwisely tight closet in our last place, I am REALLY keen to make sure all the hookups are actually accessible this time around. But I'm stumped with how we should position the dryer vent.  The back wall of this nook (the wall with the outlets) is an exterior wall, so we are planning to vent the dryer out that wall.  Our new stackable machines will arrive in a little over a week, and our contractor is coming out the week after that to cut the required hole through this exterior wall and then to install the dryer duct and the machines. Since we will have had our new washer and dryer delivered by the time he arrives, our contractor has proposed measuring the exact spot where the dryer vent is on this specific model, cutting the hole in the wall exactly there, installing whatever vent outlet thing goes through the wall, and then positioning the dryer so its vent and the wall vent outlet thing are perfectly aligned and then just shoving the washer/dryer straight into the wall vent outlet thing. I understand his point that there will be no shorter, straighter run possible with duct, but: Before he proposed that plan, I had been assuming we'd cut the hole through the wall somewhere high on the wall -- maybe roughly level with where the electrical outlets are -- because up high is the only area we'll be able to reach once the machines are in place. I figured we'd use rigid ducts, attach a 90 to the machine, then attach a vertical straight to that 90, then shove the machines in place, and then attach a 90 at the top where it would exit through the wall. But of course that adds a couple feet and two 90-degree turns compared to my contractor's plan, and for the life of me, I can't find examples when I google of how people usually run ducts in this situation. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~95565269", "author_name": "NIC interior", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~95565269", "date": "2023-11-29", "text": "Hallo, alles Gute zum Einzug! In der ersten Zeit ist es immer etwas unaufger\u00e4umt, bis sich alles zurechtgeruckelt hat. Wenn alles seinen Platz gefunden hat, wird es schon viel besser wirken. Aber da gibt es noch ein paar Knackpunkte und Sie sehen mir hoffentlich meine Offenheit nach: - Streichen Sie den Raum in einem weichen Cremeton. (Ja, das tut weh, aber das Zironengelb in der Kombi mit dem vielen Holz und dem Dunkelblau ist nicht gem\u00fctlich.) - R\u00fccken Sie das Sofa von der Wand weg, da ist Platz genug und es gibt keinen Grund, warum Sie das gro\u00dfe M\u00f6bel so in die Raumecke quetschen. Das gilt auch f\u00fcr die Leuchte. - G\u00f6nnen Sie dem Sofa einen Teppich. Der muss in der Gr\u00f6\u00dfe dem M\u00f6bel entsprechen. Wenn er zu klein ist, sieht es piefkig aus und macht den Raum optisch kleiner. Bei einem Modell mit Beinen stelle ich das M\u00f6bel auch gerne ganz darauf, aber wenigstens so weit, dass man das Ende des Teppichs nicht mehr erkennt, wenn man auf das Sofa schaut. Probieren Sie das mit einer Zeitung aus, das ist besser als mit einem Zollstock, weil Sie dann eine Fl\u00e4che sehen. - Es gibt Wandleuchten, die weicheres Licht machen als Ihre (das mag auch am Bild liegen, aber das Format der Leuchte ist auch nicht sehr gl\u00fccklich. So, wie sie jetzt h\u00e4ngt, verlangt sie danach, dass etwas L\u00e4ngliches unter ihr steht, eine Sideboard z.B..). - Den Schrank w\u00fcrde ich dort hinstellen, wo das Fass steht (das d\u00fcrfte verschwinden). Denn auch dieses M\u00f6bel steht in die Ecke gequetscht, dabei ist genug Raum da. Wenn Sie das n\u00e4chste Mal Kastenm\u00f6bel kaufen, w\u00fcrde ich eine schlichte Lackoberfl\u00e4che w\u00e4hlen (Lack hei\u00dft nicht hochgl\u00e4nzend), dann stehen sie in keiner Konkurrenz mehr zu Boden und Decke. Es ist jetzt sehr viel Struktur und auch das bringt Unruhe. - Die einsame Pflanze vor dem TV M\u00f6bel freut sich \u00fcber einen gr\u00f6\u00dferen Topf, dann steht sie auch lieber auf dem Boden. Auch die Fensterbankdeko k\u00f6nnte etwas anders gruppiert werden. Probieren Sie mal, wie es aussieht, wenn es nicht so regelm\u00e4\u00dfig aufgereiht ist und au\u00dfer Planzen auch mal eine kleine Leuchte oder eine Figur dort stehen. - Last not least: Gardinen bringen eine Menge Gem\u00fctlichkeit. Rechts und links vom Fenster jeweils ein Schal, bodenlang. In Ihrem Zimmer w\u00fcrde ich Stangen statt Schienen w\u00e4hlen, da der Sturz sehr hoch ist und die Dekoration immer einen Bezug zum Fenster haben muss, um gut zu wirken. Und bei kleinen Fenstern sehen Stangen zudem sehr dekorativ aus. (Stangen werden an der Wand befestigt, nicht an der Decke!) W\u00e4hlen Sie einen uni, griffigen Baumwollstoff, nichts Gl\u00e4nzendes oder Transparentes. Decke und Boden haben genug Muster. Das Holz wird besser zur Wirkung kommen, wenn es einen schlichten Partner bekommt. Viel Erfolg! NIC", "images": []}}

title: I tried a slightly new way to root cuttings inside of zip lock bags. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jacqueline9ca", "author_name": "jacqueline9CA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jacqueline9ca", "date": "2023-11-29", "text": "I am not good at rooting cuttings. I was using the \"put the cuttings in damp soil inside of an inflated one gallon zip lock bag until you see lots of roots\" system\". I only got about 1 out of 5 which did not die either before making any roots, or right after I moved it to a pot after it had enough roots. So, I grabbed 2 small clay pots (they are about 6 inches across at the top, 6 inches high, and the kind which get narrower towards the bottom). I put them into two 2 gallon zip lock bags (after filling them with potting soil, watering them and letting them drain). Then I dipped the bottom of two cuttings into rooting powder, and planted them in the pots, sprayed them with water with a bit of baking soda. Then I inflated the bags, and put my small cheap fish tank over them - two of these pots in their inflated 2 gallon zip lock bags fit under it fine, and there is plenty of room for the cuttings to grow up to 8 inches tall. My fish tank is 20 inches wide, 10 inches deep, and about 14 inches high. This sits right up to a bright window in my back porch on a long table I have there. I only use the fish tank because our back porch is our cats' \"territory\" (they have a climbing cat tree thingy out there, and their litter boxes under the table, and cat beds which are heated in the winter also on top of the table next to the fish tank with the roses. When I started out, and was using just inflated one gallon zip lock bags, they threw them on the floor several times. Thus the fish tank, which they love, and they sit up there in the summers and take naps or get a better view of the birds out the large window. The pic below was taken without the 2 gallon zip lock bags, and the system works much better after I added them (no idea why - more insulation, possibly?). title: (OT)  "You have terrible soil" | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2023-11-30", "text": "said the lady at the nursery this morning, when I was buying shrubs for hedging there.  It was said without malice, by someone who knows the area, and it was perfectly correct.  We do have terrible soil:  gray clay poor in organic matter; or rocks with some plant detritus over them; or thin, root-netted soil down in the woods.  However, we also have hundreds if not thousands of shrubs, trees, subshrubs, perennials, annuals, and bulbs, living and growing and not a few doing quite well. You don't need great soil to have a great garden, though it certainly helps.  And you always need to choose with care the kinds of plants you grow.  Italian cypresses and native oaks love our poor soil, steep slope, and beating sun; phlomis and shrub germander are champions.  Cyclamen flourish in the woods, fragrant violets and primroses, and spring snowflake along the drainage.  We can't grow every plant, but we can grow quite a few, and every plant that gets established makes life a little better for the rest.  We dig and amend, even a lot, and it helps, but it's just to give the plants a start; after that they help themselves. It's taken twenty years to get from the meager field we started with, and it will need another twenty, which I likely won't have, to get the garden to a reasonable state of completion.  Meanwhile I'm having fun, and the soil is becoming more fertile and sustaining more life.  It's all good.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "tozmo1", "author_name": "tozmo1", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tozmo1", "date": "2023-12-17", "text": "Here\u2019s my home building story of 2023 that is right out of a Hallmark movie. Long story why, but recently I purchased a new build house in a subdivision to rent to a friend I\u2019ve known for decades who is the guardian of her 14 year old wheelchair bound granddaughter. Her current living situation is not ADA equipped, so care of her granddaughter is physically exhausting as anyone who has cared for a disabled person in an unequipped home knows. We tried to find something existing to modify but due to my budget, nothing could be found that wouldn\u2019t become a money pit. Our tireless realtor suggested we look at new builds. She had worked many years prior for a tract builder that had ADA plans they could turn to when needed. Unfortunately, we were told by the onsite staff of the builder she recommended that they didn\u2019t do that. She was soooo annoyed and commented only to me, \u201cThey have handicapped parking at the model so you can look but you can\u2019t actually live there.\u201d That got me thinking. Since this is a national builder headquartered in Scottsdale AZ (mecca for seniors and rollators!) I pressed on and eventually connected with an angel on earth, the VP of Sales for the builder. He said, \u201cOf course we can do that. What do you need?\u201d This builder has been nothing but accommodating. He and the VP of construction have done several site visits with my friend and her granddaughter to see her navigate the model, have drawn up plans specific to her abilities and needs, charged me for changes such as zero entry shower, pull out cabinets, etc. but aren\u2019t charging for many of the simple but necessary things like wider doors, zero entry porches into the house, raising outlets, etc. The sales staff, the construction crew and everyone involved in this build have really embraced this project to the point where the VP of Sales tells me employees approach him and ask, \u201cWhat can I do? What if I do XYZ (related to whatever is their area of responsibility)? It\u2019s been a 6 month journey of fits and starts to get to this point, a series of disappointments for the granddaughter. My friend hasn\u2019t yet told her granddaughter it\u2019s really happening. She thinks the idea has passed. But on Tuesday my friend is bringing her granddaughter to the site which is at the framing stage and will surprise her with a big \u201cTa Da! Here\u2019s your new home! You no longer have to be carried up the stairs to take a bath, have no access to many rooms in the house, can\u2019t reach cabinets, bang against the vanity, can\u2019t do your own laundry, etc.\u201d The builder\u2019s staff are going to be there to present her with her very own personalized hard hat she can wear on future visits and a Christmas tree in the living room space. Completion target is March 2024 so plenty of time for things to be less than Hallmark perfect, but I just know it\u2019s going to be awesome no matter what comes our way. I\u2019m reminded that often people can see only as far as they\u2019ve ever seen and it doesn\u2019t hurt to press that vision a bit further with kindness and an open mind and heart. Worked for me. Sometimes home building stories are pretty darn amazing. Happy Holidays and Happy New Year!", "images": []}}

title: Kitchen Cabinet Install Is A Mess! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-901988629", "author_name": "Emme Warren", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-901988629", "date": "2023-11-30", "text": "I've never been able to afford any kind of renovation before this particular project, and so I was very excited for this renovation.  I've got a small 3/2 rambler with an L-shaped kitchen that consists of only 10 cabinets (2 of them bridges). Because the house can be dark, I decided to replace the stock-sized old 80's-style oak cabinets with white shaker cabinets, no changes to the layout. My estimates came in at 3 to 4 days max for demo/install, including the counter and between $9 and $17k. My late dad having been a GC, I kept in mind \"you get what you pay for\" and also to make sure everyone was licensed and insured. I went middle-of-the road with someone who seemed legit, showed me a lot of photos of his supposed work at large \"fancy\" houses. I gave a $4k deposit for the cabinets, which I knew from other quotes would be about $2200. First, he showed up with a bunch of cabinets not on our layout, both in size and design (eg a 12\" 3-drawer base cab was there for some reason and none of my cabinets were slimmer that 15\"). He didn't go over any changes with me so I didn't know there were any changes until he'd unboxed and built them. He tried to tell me that was all the cabinet store had, then that the sizes on the layout wouldn't fit, then that they were out of the box so I had to keep them. He put them up on the walls upside down, was trying to put spacers in to make a bunch of 12\" wall cabinets fit the space then left for the weekend, upset because nothing was fitting. In 5 days he'd only hung 1 base and 1 wall cabinet. I decided to fire him, to come take his cabinets, refund me $2k and keep the rest, but his wife begged me to let them finish the job. And so I caved. We're over 3 weeks into the project that everyone gave me a 3-4 day turnaround on with no work being done for some reason this week while waiting for the counter guy. I started to look at the work and noticed that aside from no finish work being done (filling in holes, repairing chips, etc), he'd cut a huge square out of the back of the sink cabinet, there are empty screw holes everywhere, the base cabinets that are next to each other aren't level, but most concerning to me is that the wall cabinets don't appear to have been hung on studs in more than one place. One in particular, 15\" wide, only has a screw angled up in the top left corner and in the bottom left corner as well. there are no screws into anything on the right side. This appears the same in other cabinets - some only have one screw off-center top or bottom holding them on. I don't see that he used blocking or toggle bolts or anything other than black screws. I don't think this was done correctly, and with my dad having passed away last year, I don't have him to ask and I watched him install lots of kitchens over the years. title: Ideal Soil Mix for Italian Cypress? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "westes", "author_name": "westes Zone 9b California SF Bay", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/westes", "date": "2023-11-30", "text": "I have some Swane's Golden Italian Cypress, which is a yellowish variety of the standard Cupressus sempervirens.   These will start off in a raised bed so I can create an ideal soil mix.   The raised bed is on top of a clay loam soil (San Francisco Bay Area zone 9b).    Would a bark-based soil mix work well? I buy a mix from Ciardella's Garden Supply in Palo Alto named Ciardella's Mix.   It's somewhat comparable to the 5-1-1 mix by @tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a).   This is a very well-drained soil, highly organic, and has good structure.   I have found most container plants thrive in it, and I have a few raised beds with this as the soil layer over clay loam, and the plants in those beds have thrived.   I realize that some do not like to create layers of soil and prefer to just use the normal clay loam as the raised bed soil.    The mix I am using is not expensive by the cubic yard and money should not be a reason to reject it.   Is there any reason to reject using this as a raised bed soil mix for Italian Cypress?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/11d282ae05691c97_7418-w500-h750-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2023-12-01", "text": "When I made the soil for my raised beds, it ended up having about a 75-80% organic fraction by volume. If I had it to do over, I would have limited the organic fraction to less than 20% and likely somewhere between 10-15%.  I was and still am very happy with its productivity, but the annual shrinkage due to gassing off is considerable, and it requires watering every day or every other day in the summer. Layering media in RBs isn't an issue if the particle size in the layer immediately above is larger. In order for water to perch in a RB, the soil in the RB would need to be 1/2 (or less) the size of the soil below, and that would be uncommon. Water won't perch in stratified soils unless particles in the lower layer are >2.1x the size of the particles in the upper strata.
